## [W4] Wikipedia: Genetic linkage
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Genetic_linkage&oldid=1377987233 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W4.1] Genetic linkage is the tendency of DNA sequences that are close together on a chromosome to be inherited together during the meiosis phase of sexual reproduction.
- [W4.2] Two genetic markers that are physically near to each other are unlikely to be separated onto different chromatids during chromosomal crossover, and are therefore said to be more linked than markers that are far apart.
- [W4.3] In other words, the nearer two genes are on a chromosome, the lower the chance of recombination between them, and the more likely they are to be inherited together.
- [W4.4] Markers on different chromosomes are perfectly unlinked, although the penetrance of potentially deleterious alleles may be influenced by the presence of other alleles, and these other alleles may be located on other chromosomes than that on which a particular potentially deleterious allele is located.
- [W4.5] Genetic linkage is the most prominent exception to Gregor Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.
- [W4.6] The first experiment to demonstrate linkage was carried out in 1905.
- [W4.7] At the time, the reason why certain traits tend to be inherited together was unknown.
- [W4.8] Later work revealed that genes are physical structures related by physical distance.
- [W4.9] The typical unit of genetic linkage is the centimorgan (cM).
- [W4.10] A distance of 1 cM between two markers means that the markers are separated to different chromosomes on average once per 100 meiotic product, thus once per 50 meioses.
- [W4.11] Gregor Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment states that every trait is inherited independently of every other trait.
- [W4.12] But shortly after Mendel's work was rediscovered, exceptions to this rule were found.
- [W4.13] In 1905, the British geneticists William Bateson, Edith Rebecca Saunders and Reginald Punnett cross-bred pea plants in experiments similar to Mendel's.
- [W4.14] They were interested in trait inheritance in the sweet pea and were studying two genes—the gene for flower colour (P, purple, and p, red) and the gene affecting the shape of pollen grains (L, long, and l, round).
- [W4.15] They crossed the pure lines PPLL and ppll and then self-crossed the resulting PpLl lines.
- [W4.16] According to Mendelian genetics, the expected phenotypes would occur in a 9:3:3:1 ratio of PL:Pl:pL:pl.
- [W4.17] To their surprise, they observed an increased frequency of PL and pl and a decreased frequency of Pl and pL:
- [W4.18] Their experiment revealed linkage between the P and L alleles and the p and l alleles.
- [W4.19] The frequency of P occurring together with L and p occurring together with l is greater than that of the recombinant Pl and pL.
- [W4.20] The recombination frequency is more difficult to compute in an F2 cross than a backcross, but the lack of fit between observed and expected numbers of progeny in the above table indicate it is less than 50%.
- [W4.21] This indicated that two factors interacted in some way to create this difference by masking the appearance of the other two phenotypes.
- [W4.22] This led to the conclusion that some traits are related to each other because of their near proximity to each other on a chromosome.
- [W4.23] The understanding of linkage was expanded by the work of Thomas Hunt Morgan.
- [W4.24] Morgan's observation that the amount of crossing over between linked genes differs led to the idea that crossover frequency might indicate the distance separating genes on the chromosome.
- [W4.25] The centimorgan, which expresses the frequency of crossing over, is named in his honour.
- [W4.26] A linkage map (also known as a genetic map) is a table for a species or experimental population that shows the position of its known genes or genetic markers relative to each other in terms of recombination frequency, rather than a specific physical distance along each chromosome.
- [W4.27] Linkage maps were first developed by Alfred Sturtevant, a student of Thomas Hunt Morgan.
- [W4.28] A linkage map is a map based on the frequencies of recombination between markers during crossover of homologous chromosomes.
- [W4.29] The greater the frequency of recombination (segregation) between two genetic markers, the further apart they are assumed to be.
- [W4.30] Conversely, the lower the frequency of recombination between the markers, the smaller the physical distance between them.
- [W4.31] Historically, the markers originally used were detectable phenotypes (enzyme production, eye colour) derived from coding DNA sequences; eventually, confirmed or assumed noncoding DNA sequences such as microsatellites or those generating restriction fragment length polymorphisms (RFLPs) have been used.
- [W4.32] Linkage maps help researchers to locate other markers, such as other genes by testing for genetic linkage of the already known markers.
- [W4.33] In the early stages of developing a linkage map, the data are used to assemble linkage groups, a set of genes which are known to be linked.
- [W4.34] As knowledge advances, more markers can be added to a group, until the group covers an entire chromosome.
- [W4.35] For well-studied organisms the linkage groups correspond one-to-one with the chromosomes.
- [W4.36] A linkage map is not a physical map (such as a radiation reduced hybrid map) or gene map.
- [W4.37] Linkage analysis is a genetic method that searches for chromosomal segments that cosegregate with the ailment phenotype through families.
- [W4.38] It can be used to map genes for both binary and quantitative traits.
- [W4.39] Linkage analysis may be either parametric (if we know the relationship between phenotypic and genetic similarity) or non-parametric.
- [W4.40] Parametric linkage analysis is the traditional approach, whereby the probability that a gene important for a disease is linked to a genetic marker is studied through the LOD score, which assesses the probability that a given pedigree, where the disease and the marker are cosegregating, is due to the existence of linkage (with a given linkage value) or to chance.
- [W4.41] Non-parametric linkage analysis, in turn, studies the probability of an allele being identical by descent with itself.
- [W4.42] Parametric linkage analysis
- [W4.43] The LOD score (logarithm (base 10) of odds), developed by Newton Morton, is a statistical test often used for linkage analysis in human, animal, and plant populations.
- [W4.44] The LOD score compares the likelihood of obtaining the test data if the two loci are indeed linked, to the likelihood of observing the same data purely by chance (that is, it is (the log of) the likelihood ratio).
- [W4.45] Thus, one can add the LOD score to the log odds of the prior probability for the hypothesis to update it to the posterior log odds as prescribed by Bayes' law.
- [W4.46] That is, LOD scores are precisely the strength of evidence (in base 10 instead of bits) for linkage of an amount equal to the observed amount (essentially, a  maximum likelihood or maximum a posteriori value).
- [W4.47] Positive LOD scores favour the presence of linkage, whereas negative LOD scores indicate that linkage is less likely.
- [W4.48] Computerised LOD score analysis is a simple way to analyse complex family pedigrees in order to determine the linkage between Mendelian traits (or between a trait and a marker, or two markers).
- [W4.49] The method is described in greater detail by Strachan and Read.[1] Briefly, it works as follows:
- [W4.50] Make a number of estimates of recombination frequency
- [W4.51] Calculate a LOD score for each estimate
- [W4.52] The estimate with the highest LOD score will be considered the best estimate
- [W4.53] The LOD score is calculated as follows:
- [W4.54] probability of birth sequence with a given linkage value
- [W4.55] probability of birth sequence with no linkage
- [W4.56] {\displaystyle {\text{LOD}}=Z=\log _{10}{\frac {\text{probability of birth sequence with a given linkage value}}{\text{probability of birth sequence with no linkage}}}=\log _{10}{\frac {(1-\theta )^{NR}\times \theta ^{R}}{0.5^{NR+R}}}}
- [W4.57] NR denotes the number of non-recombinant offspring, and R denotes the number of recombinant offspring.
- [W4.58] The reason 0.5 is used in the denominator is that any alleles that are completely unlinked (e.g. alleles on separate chromosomes) have a 50% chance of recombination, due to independent assortment. θ is the recombinant fraction, i.e. the fraction of births in which recombination has happened between the studied genetic marker and the putative gene associated with the disease.
- [W4.59] Thus, it is equal to R / (NR + R).
- [W4.60] By convention, a LOD score greater than 3.0 is considered evidence for linkage, as it indicates 1000 to 1 odds that the linkage being observed did not occur by chance.
- [W4.61] On the other hand, a LOD score less than −2.0 is considered evidence to exclude linkage.
- [W4.62] Although it is very unlikely that a LOD score of 3 would be obtained from a single pedigree, the mathematical properties of the test allow data from a number of pedigrees to be combined by summing their LOD scores.
- [W4.63] A LOD score of 3 translates to a p-value of approximately 0.05, and no multiple testing correction (e.g.
- [W4.64] Bonferroni correction) is required.
- [W4.65] Linkage analysis has a number of methodological and theoretical limitations that can significantly increase the type-1 error rate and reduce the power to map human quantitative trait loci (QTL).
- [W4.66] While linkage analysis was successfully used to identify genetic variants that contribute to rare disorders such as Huntington disease, it did not perform that well when applied to more common disorders such as heart disease or different forms of cancer.
- [W4.67] An explanation for this is that the genetic mechanisms affecting common disorders are different from those causing some rare disorders.
- [W4.68] Recombination frequency is a measure of genetic linkage and is used in the creation of a genetic linkage map.
- [W4.69] Recombination frequency (θ) is the frequency with which a single chromosomal crossover will take place between two genes during meiosis.
- [W4.70] A centimorgan (cM) is a unit that describes a recombination frequency of 1%.
- [W4.71] In this way we can measure the genetic distance between two loci, based upon their recombination frequency.
- [W4.72] This is a good estimate of the real distance.
- [W4.73] Double crossovers would turn into no recombination.
- [W4.74] In this case we cannot tell if crossovers took place.
- [W4.75] If the loci we're analysing are very close (less than 7 cM) a double crossover is very unlikely.
- [W4.76] When distances become higher, the likelihood of a double crossover increases.
- [W4.77] As the likelihood of a double crossover increases one could systematically underestimate the genetic distance between two loci, unless one used an appropriate mathematical model.
- [W4.78] Double linkage is more of a historical concern for plants.
- [W4.79] In animals, double crossover happens rarely.
- [W4.80] In humans, for example, one chromosome has two crossovers on average during meiosis.
- [W4.81] Furthermore, modern geneticists have enough genes that only nearby genes need to be linkage-analyzed, unlike the early days when only a few genes were known.
- [W4.82] During meiosis, chromosomes assort randomly into gametes, such that the segregation of alleles of one gene is independent of alleles of another gene.
- [W4.83] This is stated in Mendel's Second Law and is known as the law of independent assortment.
- [W4.84] The law of independent assortment always holds true for genes that are located on different chromosomes, but for genes that are on the same chromosome, it does not always hold true.
- [W4.85] As an example of independent assortment, consider the crossing of the pure-bred homozygote parental strain with genotype AABB with a different pure-bred strain with genotype aabb.
- [W4.86] A and a and B and b represent the alleles of genes A and B.
- [W4.87] Crossing these homozygous parental strains will result in F1 generation offspring that are double heterozygotes with genotype AaBb.
- [W4.88] The F1 offspring AaBb produces gametes that are AB, Ab, aB, and ab with equal frequencies (25%) because the alleles of gene A assort independently of the alleles for gene B during meiosis.
- [W4.89] Note that 2 of the 4 gametes (50%)—Ab and aB—were not present in the parental generation.
- [W4.90] These gametes represent recombinant gametes.
- [W4.91] Recombinant gametes are those gametes that differ from both of the haploid gametes that made up the original diploid cell.
- [W4.92] In this example, the recombination frequency is 50% since 2 of the 4 gametes were recombinant gametes.
- [W4.93] The recombination frequency will be 50% when two genes are located on different chromosomes or when they are widely separated on the same chromosome.
- [W4.94] This is a consequence of independent assortment.
- [W4.95] When two genes are close together on the same chromosome, they do not assort independently and are said to be linked.
- [W4.96] Whereas genes located on different chromosomes assort independently and have a recombination frequency of 50%, linked genes have a recombination frequency that is less than 50%.
- [W4.97] As an example of linkage, consider the classic experiment by William Bateson and Reginald Punnett.
- [W4.98] They were interested in trait inheritance in the sweet pea and were studying two genes—the gene for flower colour (P, purple, and p, red) and the gene affecting the shape of pollen grains (L, long, and l, round).
- [W4.99] They crossed the pure lines PPLL and ppll and then self-crossed the resulting PpLl lines.
- [W4.100] According to Mendelian genetics, the expected phenotypes would occur in a 9:3:3:1 ratio of PL:Pl:pL:pl.
- [W4.101] To their surprise, they observed an increased frequency of PL and pl and a decreased frequency of Pl and pL (see table below).
- [W4.102] Their experiment revealed linkage between the P and L alleles and the p and l alleles.
- [W4.103] The frequency of P occurring together with L and with p occurring together with l is greater than that of the recombinant Pl and pL.
- [W4.104] The recombination frequency is more difficult to compute in an F2 cross than a backcross, but the lack of fit between observed and expected numbers of progeny in the above table indicate it is less than 50%.
- [W4.105] The progeny in this case received two dominant alleles linked on one chromosome (referred to as coupling or cis arrangement).
- [W4.106] However, after crossover, some progeny could have received one parental chromosome with a dominant allele for one trait (e.g.
- [W4.107] Purple) linked to a recessive allele for a second trait (e.g. round) with the opposite being true for the other parental chromosome (e.g. red and Long).
- [W4.108] This is referred to as repulsion or a trans arrangement.
- [W4.109] The phenotype here would still be purple and long but a test cross of this individual with the recessive parent would produce progeny with much greater proportion of the two crossover phenotypes.
- [W4.110] While such a problem may not seem likely from this example, unfavourable repulsion linkages do appear when breeding for disease resistance in some crops.
- [W4.111] The two possible arrangements, cis and trans, of alleles in a double heterozygote are referred to as gametic phases, and phasing is the process of determining which of the two is present in a given individual.
- [W4.112] When two genes are located on the same chromosome, the chance of a crossover producing recombination between the genes is related to the distance between the two genes.
- [W4.113] Thus, the use of recombination frequencies has been used to develop linkage maps or genetic maps.
- [W4.114] However, recombination frequency tends to underestimate the distance between two linked genes.
- [W4.115] This is because as the two genes are located farther apart, the chance of double or even number of crossovers between them also increases.
- [W4.116] Double or even number of crossovers between the two genes results in them being cosegregated to the same gamete, yielding a parental progeny instead of the expected recombinant progeny.
- [W4.117] As mentioned above, the Kosambi and Haldane transformations attempt to correct for multiple crossovers.
- [W4.118] Linkage of genetic sites within a gene
- [W4.119] In the early 1950s the prevailing view was that the genes in a chromosome are discrete entities, indivisible by genetic recombination and arranged like beads on a string.
- [W4.120] During 1955 to 1959, Benzer performed genetic recombination experiments using rII mutants of bacteriophage T4.
- [W4.121] He found that, on the basis of recombination tests, the sites of mutation could be mapped in a linear order.
- [W4.122] This result provided evidence for the key idea that the gene has a linear structure equivalent to a length of DNA with many sites that can independently mutate.
- [W4.123] Edgar et al. performed mapping experiments with r mutants of bacteriophage T4 showing that recombination frequencies between rII mutants are not strictly additive.
- [W4.124] The recombination frequency from a cross of two rII mutants (a x d) is usually less than the sum of recombination frequencies for adjacent internal sub-intervals (a x b) + (b x c) + (c x d).
- [W4.125] Although not strictly additive, a systematic relationship was observed that likely reflects the underlying molecular mechanism of genetic recombination.
- [W4.126] Variation of recombination frequency
- [W4.127] While recombination of chromosomes is an essential process during meiosis, there is a large range of frequency of cross overs across organisms and within species.
- [W4.128] Sexually dimorphic rates of recombination are termed heterochiasmy, and are observed more often than a common rate between male and females.
- [W4.129] In mammals, females often have a higher rate of recombination compared to males.
- [W4.130] It is theorised that there are unique selections acting or meiotic drivers which influence the difference in rates.
- [W4.131] The difference in rates may also reflect the vastly different environments and conditions of meiosis in oogenesis and spermatogenesis.
- [W4.132] Genes affecting recombination frequency
- [W4.133] Mutations in genes that encode proteins involved in the processing of DNA often affect recombination frequency.
- [W4.134] In bacteriophage T4, mutations that reduce expression of the replicative DNA polymerase [gene product 43 (gp43)] increase recombination (decrease linkage) several fold.
- [W4.135] The increase in recombination may be due to replication errors by the defective DNA polymerase that are themselves recombination events such as template switches, i.e. copy choice recombination events.
- [W4.136] Recombination is also increased by mutations that reduce the expression of DNA ligase (gp30) and dCMP hydroxymethylase (gp42), two enzymes employed in DNA synthesis.
- [W4.137] Recombination is reduced (linkage increased) by mutations in genes that encode proteins with nuclease functions (gp46 and gp47) and a DNA-binding protein (gp32)  Mutation in the bacteriophage uvsX gene also substantially reduces recombination.
- [W4.138] The uvsX gene is analogous to the well studied recA gene of Escherichia coli that plays a central role in recombination.
- [W4.139] With very large pedigrees or with very dense genetic marker data, such as from whole-genome sequencing, it is possible to precisely locate recombinations.
- [W4.140] With this type of genetic analysis, a meiosis indicator is assigned to each position of the genome for each meiosis in a pedigree.
- [W4.141] The indicator indicates which copy of the parental chromosome contributes to the transmitted gamete at that position.
- [W4.142] For example, if the allele from the 'first' copy of the parental chromosome is transmitted, a '0' might be assigned to that meiosis.
- [W4.143] If the allele from the 'second' copy of the parental chromosome is transmitted, a '1' would be assigned to that meiosis.
- [W4.144] The two alleles in the parent came, one each, from two grandparents.
- [W4.145] These indicators are then used to determine identical-by-descent (IBD) states or inheritance states, which are in turn used to identify genes responsible for diseases.
- [W4.146] Griffiths AJF; Miller JH; Suzuki DT; Lewontin RC; et al.
- [W4.147] An Introduction to Genetic Analysis (5th ed.).
- [W4.148] Poehlman JM; Sleper DA (1995).
- [W4.149] Breeding Field Crops (4th ed.).

## [W5] Wikipedia: Homologous chromosome
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Homologous_chromosome&oldid=1375262078 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W5.1] Homologous chromosomes or homologs are a set of one maternal and one paternal chromosome that pair up with each other inside a cell during meiosis.
- [W5.2] Homologs have the same genes in the same loci but possibly different alleles, where they provide points along each chromosome that enable a pair of chromosomes to align correctly with each other before separating during meiosis.
- [W5.3] This is the basis for Mendelian inheritance, which characterizes inheritance patterns of genetic material from an organism to its offspring parent developmental cell at the given time and area.
- [W5.4] Chromosomes are linear arrangements of condensed deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and histone proteins, which form a complex called chromatin.
- [W5.5] Homologous chromosomes are made up of chromosome pairs of approximately the same length, centromere position, and staining pattern, for genes with the same corresponding loci.
- [W5.6] One homologous chromosome is inherited from the organism's mother; the other is inherited from the organism's father.
- [W5.7] After meiosis occurs within the daughter cells, they have the correct number of genes which are a mix of the two parents' genes.
- [W5.8] In diploid (2n) organisms, the genome is composed of one set of each homologous chromosome pair, as compared to tetraploid organisms which may have two sets of each homologous chromosome pair.
- [W5.9] The alleles on the homologous chromosomes may be different, resulting in different phenotypes of the same genes.
- [W5.10] This mixing of maternal and paternal traits is enhanced by crossing over during meiosis, wherein lengths of chromosomal arms and the DNA they contain within a homologous chromosome pair are exchanged with one another.
- [W5.11] Early in the 1900s, William Bateson and Reginald Punnett were studying genetic inheritance and they noted that some combinations of alleles appeared more frequently than others.
- [W5.12] That data and information was further explored by Thomas Morgan.
- [W5.13] Using test cross experiments, he revealed that, for a single parent, the alleles of genes near to one another along the length of the chromosome move together.
- [W5.14] Using this logic he concluded that the two genes he was studying were located on homologous chromosomes.
- [W5.15] Later on during the 1930s, Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock were studying meiosis in corn cells and examining gene loci on corn chromosomes.
- [W5.16] Creighton and McClintock discovered that the new allele combinations present in the offspring and the event of crossing over were directly related.
- [W5.17] This proved interchromosomal genetic recombination.
- [W5.18] Homologous chromosomes are pairs of chromosomes in a diploid organism that have similar genes, although not necessarily identical.
- [W5.19] There are two main properties of homologous chromosomes: 1) the length of chromosomal arms and 2) the placement of the centromere.
- [W5.20] The actual length of the arm, in accordance with the gene locations, is critically important for proper alignment.
- [W5.21] Centromere placement on the chromosome can be characterized by four main arrangements, either metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric, or telocentric.
- [W5.22] Both of these properties (i.e., the length of chromosomal arms, and the placement of the chromosomal centromere) are the main factors for creating structural homology between chromosomes.
- [W5.23] Therefore, when two chromosomes containing the relatively same structure exist (e.g., maternal chromosome 15 and paternal chromosome 15), they are able to pair together via the process of synapsis to form homologous chromosomes.
- [W5.24] Since homologous chromosomes are not identical and do not originate from the same organism, they are different from sister chromatids.
- [W5.25] Sister chromatids result after DNA replication has occurred, and thus are identical, side-by-side duplicates of each other.
- [W5.26] Humans have a total of 46 chromosomes, but there are only 22 pairs of homologous autosomal chromosomes.
- [W5.27] The additional 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes, X and Y.
- [W5.28] In humans, the 22 pairs of homologous autosomal chromosomes contain the same genes but may code for different traits in their allelic forms, as one was inherited from the mother and one from the father.
- [W5.29] So, humans have two sets of 23 chromosomes in each cell that contains a nucleus.
- [W5.30] One set of 23 chromosomes (n) is from the parent ovum (22 autosomes, 1 sex chromosome (X only)) and one set of 23 chromosomes (n) is from the parent spermatozoon (22 autosomes, 1 sex chromosome (X or Y)).
- [W5.31] Ultimately, this means that humans are diploid (2n) organisms.
- [W5.32] Homologous chromosomes are important in the processes of meiosis and mitosis.
- [W5.33] They allow for the recombination and random segregation of genetic material from the mother and father into new cells.
- [W5.34] Meiosis is a round of two cell divisions that results in four haploid daughter cells that each contain half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
- [W5.35] It reduces the chromosome number in a germ cell by half by first separating the homologous chromosomes in meiosis I and then the sister chromatids in meiosis II.
- [W5.36] The process of meiosis I is generally longer than meiosis II because it takes more time for the chromatin to replicate and for the homologous chromosomes to be properly oriented and segregated by the processes of pairing and synapsis in meiosis I.
- [W5.37] During meiosis, genetic recombination (by random segregation) and crossing over produces daughter cells that each contain different combinations of maternally and paternally coded genes.
- [W5.38] This recombination of genes allows for the introduction of new allele pairings and genetic variation.
- [W5.39] Genetic variation among organisms helps make a population more stable by providing a wider range of genetic traits for natural selection to act on.
- [W5.40] In prophase I of meiosis I, each chromosome is aligned with its homologous partner and pairs completely.
- [W5.41] In prophase I, the DNA has already undergone replication so each chromosome consists of two identical chromatids connected by a common centromere.
- [W5.42] During the zygotene stage of prophase I, the homologous chromosomes pair up with each other.
- [W5.43] This pairing occurs by a synapsis process where the synaptonemal complex – a protein scaffold – is assembled and joins the homologous chromosomes along their lengths.
- [W5.44] Cohesin crosslinking occurs between the homologous chromosomes and helps them resist being pulled apart until anaphase.
- [W5.45] Genetic crossing-over, a type of recombination, occurs during the pachytene stage of prophase I.
- [W5.46] In addition, another type of recombination referred to as synthesis-dependent strand annealing (SDSA) frequently occurs.
- [W5.47] SDSA recombination involves information exchange between paired homologous chromatids, but not physical exchange.
- [W5.48] SDSA recombination does not cause crossing-over.
- [W5.49] In the process of crossing-over, genes are exchanged by the breaking and union of homologous portions of the chromosomes' lengths.
- [W5.50] Structures called chiasmata are the site of the exchange.
- [W5.51] Chiasmata physically link the homologous chromosomes once crossing over occurs and throughout the process of chromosomal segregation during meiosis.
- [W5.52] Both the non-crossover and crossover types of recombination function as processes for repairing DNA damage, particularly double-strand breaks.
- [W5.53] At the diplotene stage of prophase I the synaptonemal complex disassembles before which will allow the homologous chromosomes to separate, while the sister chromatids stay associated by their centromeres.
- [W5.54] In metaphase I of meiosis I, the pairs of homologous chromosomes, also known as bivalents or tetrads, line up in a random order along the metaphase plate.
- [W5.55] The random orientation is another way for cells to introduce genetic variation.
- [W5.56] Meiotic spindles emanating from opposite spindle poles attach to each of the homologs (each pair of sister chromatids) at the kinetochore.
- [W5.57] In anaphase I of meiosis I the homologous chromosomes are pulled apart from each other.
- [W5.58] The homologs are cleaved by the enzyme separase to release the cohesin that held the homologous chromosome arms together.
- [W5.59] This allows the chiasmata to release and the homologs to move to opposite poles of the cell.
- [W5.60] The homologous chromosomes are now randomly segregated into two daughter cells that will undergo meiosis II to produce four haploid daughter germ cells.
- [W5.61] After the tetrads of homologous chromosomes are separated in meiosis I, the sister chromatids from each pair are separated.
- [W5.62] The two haploid daughter cells (the number of chromosomes has been reduced to half: earlier two sets of chromosomes were present, but now each set exists in two different daughter cells that have arisen from the single diploid parent cell by meiosis I) resulting from meiosis I undergo another cell division in meiosis II but without another round of chromosomal replication.
- [W5.63] The sister chromatids in the two daughter cells are pulled apart during anaphase II by nuclear spindle fibers, resulting in four haploid daughter cells.
- [W5.64] Homologous chromosomes do not function the same in mitosis as they do in meiosis.
- [W5.65] Prior to every single mitotic division a cell undergoes, the chromosomes in the parent cell replicate themselves.
- [W5.66] The homologous chromosomes within the cell will ordinarily not pair up and undergo genetic recombination with each other.
- [W5.67] Instead, the replicants, or sister chromatids, will line up along the metaphase plate and then separate in the same way as meiosis II – by being pulled apart at their centromeres by nuclear mitotic spindles.
- [W5.68] If any crossing over does occur between sister chromatids during mitosis, it does not produce any new recombinant genotypes.
- [W5.69] Homologous pairing in most contexts will refer to germline cells, however also takes place in somatic cells.
- [W5.70] For example, in humans, somatic cells have very tightly regulated homologous pairing (separated into chromosomal territories, and pairing at specific loci under control of developmental signalling).
- [W5.71] Other species however (notably Drosophila) exhibit homologous pairing much more frequently.
- [W5.72] In Drosophila the homologous pairing supports a gene regulatory phenomenon called transvection in which an allele on one chromosome affects the expression of the homologous allele on the homologous chromosome.
- [W5.73] One notable function of this is the sexually dimorphic regulation of X-linked genes.
- [W5.74] There are severe repercussions when chromosomes do not segregate properly.
- [W5.75] Faulty segregation can lead to fertility problems, embryo death, birth defects, and cancer.
- [W5.76] Though the mechanisms for pairing and adhering homologous chromosomes vary among organisms, proper functioning of those mechanisms is imperative in order for the final genetic material to be sorted correctly.
- [W5.77] Proper homologous chromosome separation in meiosis I is crucial for sister chromatid separation in meiosis II.
- [W5.78] A failure to separate properly is known as nondisjunction.
- [W5.79] There are two main types of nondisjunction that occur: trisomy and monosomy.
- [W5.80] Trisomy is caused by the presence of one additional chromosome in the zygote as compared to the normal number, and monosomy is characterized by the presence of one fewer chromosome in the zygote as compared to the normal number.
- [W5.81] If this uneven division occurs in meiosis I, then none of the daughter cells will have proper chromosomal distribution and non-typical effects can ensue, including Down syndrome.
- [W5.82] Unequal division can also occur during the second meiotic division.
- [W5.83] Nondisjunction which occurs at this stage can result in normal daughter cells and deformed cells.
- [W5.84] While the main function of homologous chromosomes is their use in nuclear division, they are also used in repairing double-strand breaks of DNA.
- [W5.85] These double-stranded breaks may occur in replicating DNA and are most often the result of interaction of DNA with naturally occurring damaging molecules such as reactive oxygen species.
- [W5.86] Homologous chromosomes can repair this damage by aligning themselves with chromosomes of the same genetic sequence.
- [W5.87] Once the base pairs have been matched and oriented correctly between the two strands, the homologous chromosomes perform a process that is very similar to recombination, or crossing over as seen in meiosis.
- [W5.88] Part of the intact DNA sequence overlaps with that of the damaged chromosome's sequence.
- [W5.89] Replication proteins and complexes are then recruited to the site of damage, allowing for repair and proper replication to occur.
- [W5.90] Through this functioning, double-strand breaks can be repaired and DNA can function normally.
- [W5.91] Current and future research on the subject of homologous chromosome is heavily focused on the roles of various proteins during recombination or during DNA repair.
- [W5.92] In a recently published article by Pezza et al. the protein known as HOP2 is responsible for both homologous chromosome synapsis as well as double-strand break repair via homologous recombination.
- [W5.93] The deletion of HOP2 in mice has large repercussions in meiosis.
- [W5.94] Other current studies focus on specific proteins involved in homologous recombination as well.
- [W5.95] There is ongoing research concerning the ability of homologous chromosomes to repair double-strand DNA breaks.
- [W5.96] Researchers are investigating the possibility of exploiting this capability for regenerative medicine.
- [W5.97] This medicine could be very prevalent in relation to cancer, as DNA damage is thought to be contributor to carcinogenesis.
- [W5.98] Manipulating the repair function of homologous chromosomes might allow for bettering a cell's damage response system.
- [W5.99] While research has not yet confirmed the effectiveness of such treatment, it may become a useful therapy for cancer.

## [W6] Wikipedia: Walter Sutton
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Walter_Sutton&oldid=1372006857 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W6.1] Walter Stanborough Sutton (April 5, 1877 – November 10, 1916) was an American geneticist and biologist whose most significant contribution to present-day biology was his theory that the Mendelian laws of inheritance could be applied to chromosomes at the cellular level of living organisms.
- [W6.2] This is now known as the Boveri–Sutton chromosome theory.
- [W6.3] Sutton was born in Utica, New York, and was raised on a farm as the fifth of seven sons to Judge William B.
- [W6.4] Sutton and his wife, Agnes Black Sutton, in Russell, Kansas.
- [W6.5] On the farm, he developed a mechanical aptitude by maintaining and repairing farm equipment, an aptitude that proved helpful later as he worked on oil drilling rigs and with medical instrumentation.
- [W6.6] After graduating high school in Russell, he enrolled at the University of Kansas in engineering in 1896.
- [W6.7] Following the death of his younger brother (John) from typhoid fever in 1897, Sutton switched his major to biology with an interest in medicine.
- [W6.8] While at the University of Kansas, both he and his older brother, William Sutton, played basketball for Dr.
- [W6.9] Sutton distinguished himself as a student by being elected to both Phi Beta Kappa and Sigma Xi and receiving both bachelor's and master's degrees by 1901.
- [W6.10] For his Masters thesis, he studied the spermatogenesis of Brachystola magna, a large grasshopper indigenous to the farmlands upon which Sutton was raised.
- [W6.11] Considering the advice of his mentor at KU, Dr.
- [W6.12] McClung, Sutton moved to Columbia University for further study of zoology under Dr.
- [W6.13] It was here that Sutton wrote his two significant works in genetics – "On the morphology of the chromosome group in Brachystola magna" and "The chromosomes in heredity".
- [W6.14] Effectively, Sutton could now explain "why the yellow dog is yellow".
- [W6.15] The German biologist Theodor Boveri independently reached the same conclusions as Sutton, and their concepts are often referred to as the Boveri–Sutton chromosome theory.
- [W6.16] Sutton's hypothesis was widely accepted by most scientists, particularly cytologists, at the time.
- [W6.17] The continued work of Thomas Hunt Morgan at Columbia brought the theory to universal acceptance by 1915 through his studies of Drosophila melanogaster, the fruit fly, even as William Bateson continued to question the theory until 1921.
- [W6.18] Sutton did not complete his PhD in Zoology as he originally planned.
- [W6.19] At the age of 26, he returned to the Kansas oil fields for 2 years.
- [W6.20] There he was able to perfect a device to start large gas engines with high pressure-gas and develop hoisting apparatuses for deep wells.
- [W6.21] Sutton's mechanical aptitudes never left him.
- [W6.22] His father finally directed him to return to his medical studies and he did so returning to Columbia University in 1905.
- [W6.23] Sutton's medical studies proceeded through the College of Physicians and Surgeons at Columbia University.
- [W6.24] While he continued to work on patents associated with oil drilling, Sutton also began at this stage to apply his mechanical aptitude to improving medical instruments.
- [W6.25] With credit for his graduate studies at both the University of Kansas and Columbia University, Sutton obtained his doctorate in medicine in 1907 graduating with "high standing".
- [W6.26] He then began an internship at Roosevelt Hospital in New York working in the surgical division headed by Dr.
- [W6.27] In addition to his clinic duties at Roosevelt Hospital, Sutton was also able to work with the Surgical Research Laboratory at the College of Physicians and Surgeons.
- [W6.28] With that support, he was able to begin developing and improving a variety of medical and surgical practices including improving anesthetic techniques, and perfecting abdominal irrigation.
- [W6.29] In 1909, Sutton returned to Kansas City, Kansas where his family had relocated and his father and brother were in law practice.
- [W6.30] Sutton was appointed assistant professor of surgery at the four-year-old University of Kansas Medical School.
- [W6.31] The tenuous nature of the appointment at the young school led him to also maintain a private practice and serve on the staff of St.
- [W6.32] Margaret's Hospital as well as the university's Bell Memorial Hospital.
- [W6.33] For six years, Sutton performed a wide range of surgeries carefully documenting the procedures.
- [W6.34] He published several articles related to these cases going back to his internship at Roosevelt.
- [W6.35] In 1911, he had accepted a commission as a First Lieutenant in the United States Army Medical reserve Corps.
- [W6.36] This eventually led to his taking a leave of absence from the university in February 1915 to serve at the American Ambulance Hospital outside Paris.
- [W6.37] Sutton and others from his days at Columbia and Roosevelt arrived at College of Juilly on February 23 where hospital facilities had been set up only 40 miles from the front lines of World War I.
- [W6.38] Within 2 months, he was surgeon-in-chief handling administrative duties in addition to his surgical responsibilities.
- [W6.39] His inventive aptitude was perhaps never more valued as he developed fluoroscopic techniques to identify and localize shrapnel within the soldier's bodies and then removed the foreign items with instruments of his own design.
- [W6.40] After his return, he documented these techniques in Binnie's Manual of Operative Surgery.
- [W6.41] Sutton's return sailing from France was on June 26, 1915, having stayed only four months, but have made a significant contribution to wartime medical treatment.
- [W6.42] Sutton died rather unexpectedly at the age of 39 due to complications from acute appendicitis.
- [W6.43] "100 Years Ago: Walter Sutton and the Chromosome Theory of Heredity".
- [W6.44] 160 (1): 1–4. doi:10.1093/genetics/160.1.1.
- [W6.45] Walter Sutton's Chromosome Theory of Heredity:  One Hundred Years Later

## [W7] Wikipedia: Eleanor Carothers
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eleanor_Carothers&oldid=1372256208 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W7.1] Estrella Eleanor Carothers (4 December 1882 – 1957) was an American zoologist, geneticist, and cytologist known for her work with grasshoppers.
- [W7.2] She discovered important physical evidence for the concept of Chromosome_segregation giving direct observational support for Mendelian independent assortment, vital to modern understanding of genetics.
- [W7.3] Carothers was born on December 4, 1883, in Newton, Kansas to Z.
- [W7.4] She studied at the Nickerson Normal College and went on to earn her Bachelor of Arts degree and her Master's degree from the University of Kansas, in 1911 and 1912 respectively.
- [W7.5] She began her career as a Pepper Fellow at Pennsylvania State University, where she stayed from 1913 to 1914.
- [W7.6] That year, she was appointed an assistant professor of zoology there, and graduated with her Ph.D. in 1916.
- [W7.7] Carothers stayed on as assistant professor until 1936, though she also had an overlapping appointment as an independent investigator for the Marine Biological Laboratory, which lasted from 1920 until 1941.
- [W7.8] In 1936 she moved to the University of Iowa and was a research associate there until 1941.
- [W7.9] Her work there was funded by the Rockefeller Foundation.
- [W7.10] While studying and teaching at the University of Pennsylvania, Carothers traveled to the southern and southwestern regions of the United States on research expeditions, held in 1915 and 1919.
- [W7.11] During her time at the University of Iowa, she completed her most important work, in the field of genetics and cytology, using grasshopper embryos to study the Chromosome_segregation of heteromorphic homologous chromosomes.
- [W7.12] This was the first physical evidence that homologous chromosomes separated independently during meiosis, which is one source of genetic variation in sexually-reproducing organisms.
- [W7.13] Carothers retired from the University of Iowa in 1941 and moved from Iowa to Kingman, Kansas, where she continued to conduct research for the Woods Hole Marine Biological Lab.
- [W7.14] In 1954, she moved to Murdock, Kansas, where she lived and researched for the remainder of her life.
- [W7.15] Carothers died in 1957 at the age of 75.
- [W7.16] In 1921, Carothers was awarded the Ellen Richards Research Prize by the Naples Table Association.
- [W7.17] She received a starred entry for her work on grasshopper embryos in the fourth edition of American Men of Science, published in 1927, a rare and significant award  for a female scientist at the time.
- [W7.18] Carothers was also elected to the National Academy of Sciences and the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia.

## [W8] Wikipedia: Oscar Hertwig
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Oscar_Hertwig&oldid=1380750250 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W8.1] Oscar Hertwig (21 April 1849 – 25 October 1922) was a German embryologist and zoologist known for his research in developmental biology and evolution.
- [W8.2] Hertwig is credited as the first person to observe sexual reproduction at the cellular level, by looking at the cells of sea urchins under the microscope.
- [W8.3] Hertwig was the elder brother of zoologist-professor Richard Hertwig (1850–1937).
- [W8.4] The Hertwig brothers were the most eminent scholars of Ernst Haeckel (and Carl Gegenbaur) from the University of Jena.
- [W8.5] They were independent of Haeckel's philosophical speculations but took his ideas positively to widen their concepts in zoology.
- [W8.6] Initially, between 1879 and 1883, they performed embryological studies, especially on the theory of the coelom (1881), the fluid-filled body cavity.
- [W8.7] These problems were based on the phylogenetic theorems of Haeckel, i.e., the biogenic theory (German = biogenetisches Grundgesetz), and the "gastraea theory".
- [W8.8] Within 10 years, the two brothers moved apart to the north and south of Germany.
- [W8.9] Oscar Hertwig later became a professor of anatomy in 1888 in Berlin; however, Richard Hertwig had moved 3 years prior, becoming a professor of zoology in Munich from 1885 to 1925, at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München (LMU), where he served the last 40 years of his 50-year career as a professor at 4 universities.
- [W8.10] Hertwig was a leader in the field of comparative and causal animal-developmental history.
- [W8.11] He also wrote a leading textbook.
- [W8.12] By studying sea urchins he proved that fertilization occurs due to the fusion of a sperm and egg cell.
- [W8.13] He recognized the role of the cell nucleus during inheritance and chromosome reduction during meiosis: in 1876, he published his findings that fertilization includes the penetration of a spermatozoon into an egg cell.
- [W8.14] Hermann Fol also observed this in the same year.
- [W8.15] Hertwig's experiments with frog eggs revealed the 'long axis rule', or Hertwig rule.
- [W8.16] According to this rule, cell divides along its long axis.
- [W8.17] In 1885 Hertwig wrote that nuclein (later called nucleic acid) is the substance responsible not only for fertilization but also for the transmission of hereditary characteristics.
- [W8.18] This early suggestion was proven correct much later in 1944 by the Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment which showed that this is indeed the role of the nucleic acid DNA.
- [W8.19] While Hertwig was interested in developmental biology and evolution, he was opposed to chance as assumed in Charles Darwin's theory.
- [W8.20] His most important theoretical book was: "Das Werden der Organismen, eine Widerlegung der Darwinschen Zufallslehre" (Jena, 1916) (translation: "The Origin of Organisms – a Refutation of Darwin's Theory of Chance").
- [W8.21] Hertwig was elected a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1903.
- [W8.22] In 1905, Hertwig was named an honorary member of the American Association for Anatomy.
- [W8.23] Hertwig is known as Oscar Hedwig in the book "Who discovered what when" by David Ellyard.
- [W8.24] A history of the discovery of fertilization for mammals including scientists like Hertwig and other workers is given by the book "The Mammalian Egg" by Austin.
- [W8.25] Die Elemente der Entwicklungslehre des Menschen und der Wirbeltiere : Anleitung und Repetitorium für Studierende und Ärzte (The elements of the developmental biology of humans and vertebrates: A guide and review for students and physicians).

## [W9] Wikipedia: Edouard Van Beneden
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edouard_Van_Beneden&oldid=1371988739 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W9.1] Édouard Joseph Louis Marie Van Beneden (5 March 1846 in Leuven – 28 April 1910 in Liège) was a Belgian embryologist, cytologist and marine biologist.
- [W9.2] He was professor of zoology at the University of Liège.
- [W9.3] He contributed to cytogenetics by his works on the roundworm Ascaris.
- [W9.4] In this work he discovered how chromosomes organized meiosis (the production of gametes).
- [W9.5] He is son of Pierre-Joseph Van Beneden, a zoologist and paleontologist.
- [W9.6] Van Beneden elucidated, together with Walther Flemming and Eduard Strasburger, the essential facts of mitosis, where, in contrast to meiosis, there is a qualitative and quantitative equality of chromosome distribution to daughter cells.
- [W9.7] Recherches sur la composition et la signification de l'œuf 1868 Full text available from Archive.org PDF
- [W9.8] La maturation de l'oeuf, la fecondation, et les premieres phases du développement embryonnaire des mammifères, d'aprés des recherches faites chez le lapin : communication préliminaire in Bulletins de l'Académie royale de Belgique.
- [W9.9] Van Beneden's father, Pierre-Joseph van Beneden (1809–1894) was also a well-known biologist.
- [W9.10] He introduced two important terms into evolutionary biology and ecology: mutualism and commensalism.

## [W10] Wikipedia: August Weismann
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=August_Weismann&oldid=1370696963 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W10.1] August Friedrich Leopold Weismann (German: [ˈvaɪsman]; 17 January 1834 – 5 November 1914) was a German evolutionary biologist.
- [W10.2] Fellow German Ernst Mayr ranked him as the second most notable evolutionary theorist of the 19th century, after Charles Darwin.
- [W10.3] Weismann became the Director of the Zoological Institute and the first Professor of Zoology at Freiburg.
- [W10.4] His main contribution involved germ plasm theory, at one time also known as Weismannism, according to which inheritance (in a multicellular animal) only takes place by means of the germ cells—the gametes such as egg cells and sperm cells.
- [W10.5] Other cells of the body—somatic cells—do not function as agents of heredity.
- [W10.6] The effect is one-way: germ cells produce somatic cells and are not affected by anything the somatic cells learn or therefore any ability an individual acquires during its life.
- [W10.7] Genetic information cannot pass from soma to germ plasm and on to the next generation.
- [W10.8] Biologists refer to this concept as the Weismann barrier.
- [W10.9] This idea, if true, rules out the inheritance of acquired characteristics as proposed by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck.
- [W10.10] However, a careful reading of Weismann's work over the span of his entire career shows that he had more nuanced views, insisting, like Darwin, that a variable environment was necessary to cause variation in the hereditary material.
- [W10.11] The idea of the Weismann barrier is central to the modern synthesis of the early 20th century, though scholars do not express it today in the same terms.
- [W10.12] In Weismann's opinion the largely random process of mutation, which must occur in the gametes (or stem cells that make them) is the only source of change for natural selection to work on.
- [W10.13] Weismann became one of the first biologists to deny Lamarckism entirely.
- [W10.14] Weismann's ideas preceded the rediscovery of Gregor Mendel's work, and though Weismann was cagey about accepting Mendelism, younger workers soon made the connection.
- [W10.15] Weismann was born a son of high school teacher Johann (Jean) Konrad Weismann (1804–1880), a graduate of ancient languages and theology, and his wife Elise (1803–1850), née Lübbren, the daughter of the county councillor and mayor of Stade, on 17 January 1834 in Frankfurt am Main.
- [W10.16] He had a typical 19th century bourgeois education, receiving music lessons from the age of four, and drafting and painting lessons from Jakob Becker (1810–1872) at the Frankfurter Städelsche Institut from the age of 14.
- [W10.17] His piano teacher was a devoted butterfly collector and introduced him to the collecting of imagos and caterpillars.
- [W10.18] But studying natural sciences was out of the question due to the cost involved and limited job prospects.
- [W10.19] A friend of the family, chemist Friedrich Wöhler (1800–1882), recommended studying medicine.
- [W10.20] A foundation from the inheritance of Weismann's mother allowed him to take up studies in Göttingen.
- [W10.21] Following his graduation in 1856, he wrote his dissertation on the synthesis of hippuric acid in the human body.
- [W10.22] Immediately after university, Weismann took on a post as assistant at the Städtische Klinik (city clinic) in Rostock.
- [W10.23] Weismann successfully submitted two manuscripts, one about hippuric acid in herbivores, and one about the salt content of the Baltic Sea, and won two prizes.
- [W10.24] The paper about the salt content dissuaded him from becoming a chemist, since he felt himself lacking in apothecarial accuracy.
- [W10.25] After a study visit to see Vienna's museums and clinics, he visited Italy (1859) and Paris (1860).
- [W10.26] He returned to Frankfurt as personal physician to the banished Archduke Stephen of Austria at Schaumburg Castle from 1861 to 1863.
- [W10.27] During the war between Austria, France and Italy in 1859, he became Chief Medical Officer in the military, and on a leave from duty he walked through Northern Italy and the County of Tyrol.
- [W10.28] After a sabbatical in Paris, he worked with Rudolf Leuckart at the University of Gießen.
- [W10.29] From 1863, he was privatdozent in comparative anatomy and zoology; from 1866 extraordinary professor; and from 1873 to 1912 full professor, first holder of the chair in zoology and director of the zoological institute at Albert Ludwig University of Freiburg in Breisgau.
- [W10.30] His earlier work was largely concerned with purely zoological investigations, one of his earliest works dealing with the development of the Diptera.
- [W10.31] Microscopical work, however, became impossible to him owing to impaired eyesight, and he turned his attention to wider problems of biological inquiry.
- [W10.32] In 1867 he married Mary Dorothea Gruber.
- [W10.33] Their son, Julius Weismann (1879–1950), was a composer.
- [W10.34] Contributions to evolutionary biology
- [W10.35] At the beginning of Weismann's preoccupation with evolutionary theory was his grappling with Christian creationism as a possible alternative.
- [W10.36] In his work Über die Berechtigung der Darwin'schen Theorie (On the justification of the Darwinian theory) he compared creationism and evolutionary theory, and concluded that many biological facts can be seamlessly accommodated within evolutionary theory, but remain puzzling if considered the result of acts of creation.
- [W10.37] After this work, Weismann accepted evolution as a fact on a par with the fundamental assumptions of astronomy (e.g.
- [W10.38] Weismann's position towards the mechanism of inheritance and its role for evolution changed during his life.
- [W10.39] Three periods can be distinguished.
- [W10.40] Weismann's work on the demarcation between germ-line and soma can scarcely be appreciated without considering the work of (mostly) German biologists during the second half of the 19th century.
- [W10.41] This was the time that the mechanisms of cell division began to be understood.
- [W10.42] Eduard Strasburger, Walther Flemming, Heinrich von Waldeyer and the Belgian Edouard Van Beneden laid the basis for the cytology and cytogenetics of the 20th century.
- [W10.43] Strasburger, the outstanding botanical physiologist of that century, coined the terms nucleoplasm and cytoplasm.
- [W10.44] He said "new cell nuclei can only arise from the division of other cell nuclei".
- [W10.45] Van Beneden discovered how chromosomes combined at meiosis, during the production of gametes, and discovered and named chromatin.
- [W10.46] Walther Flemming, the founder of cytogenetics, named mitosis, and pronounced "omnis nucleus e nucleo" (which means the same as Strasburger's dictum).
- [W10.47] The discovery of mitosis, meiosis and chromosomes is regarded as one of the 100 most important scientific discoveries of all times, and one of the 10 most important discoveries in cell biology.
- [W10.48] Meiosis was discovered and described for the first time in sea urchin eggs in 1876, by Oscar Hertwig.
- [W10.49] It was described again in 1883, at the level of chromosomes, by Van Beneden in Ascaris eggs.
- [W10.50] The significance of meiosis for reproduction and inheritance, however, was first described in 1890 by Weismann, who noted that two cell divisions were necessary to transform one diploid cell into four haploid cells if the number of chromosomes had to be maintained.
- [W10.51] Thus the work of the earlier cytologists laid the ground for Weismann, who turned his mind to the consequences for evolution, which was an aspect the cytologists had not addressed.
- [W10.52] All this took place before the rediscovery of the work of Mendel.
- [W10.53] Weismann started out believing, like many other 19th century scientists, among them Charles Darwin, that the observed variability of individuals of one species is due to the inheritance of sports (Darwin's term).
- [W10.54] He believed, as written in 1876, that transmutation of species is directly due to the influence of environment.
- [W10.55] He also wrote, "if every variation is regarded as a reaction of the organism to external conditions, as a deviation of the inherited line of development, it follows that no evolution can occur without a change of the environment".
- [W10.56] (This is close to the modern use of the concept that changes in the environment can mediate selective pressures on a population, so leading to evolutionary change.) Weismann also used the classic Lamarckian metaphor of use and disuse of an organ.
- [W10.57] Weismann came to understand during this part of his scientific career that evolution is never a perfect process and that an organism's evolutionary trajectory is constrained by its pre-existing physiology, in particular focusing on how the developmental biology of a species limited which directions it could evolve in.
- [W10.58] Weismann's first rejection of the inheritance of acquired traits was in a lecture in 1883, titled "On inheritance" ("Über die Vererbung").
- [W10.59] Again, as in his treatise on creation vs. evolution, he attempts to explain individual examples with either theory.
- [W10.60] For instance, the existence of non-reproductive castes of ants, such as workers and soldiers, cannot be explained by inheritance of acquired characters.
- [W10.61] Germ plasm theory, on the other hand, does so effortlessly.
- [W10.62] Weismann used this theory to explain Lamark's original examples for "use and disuse", such as the tendency to have degenerate wings and stronger feet in domesticated waterfowl.
- [W10.63] Weismann worked on the embryology of sea urchin eggs, and in the course of this observed different kinds of cell division, namely equatorial division and reductional division, terms he coined (Äquatorialteilung and Reduktionsteilung respectively).
- [W10.64] His germ plasm theory states that multicellular organisms consist of germ cells containing heritable information, and somatic cells that carry out ordinary bodily functions.
- [W10.65] The germ cells are influenced neither by environmental influences nor by learning or morphological changes that happen during the lifetime of an organism, which information is lost after each generation.
- [W10.66] The concept as he proposed it was referred to as Weismannism in his day, for example in the book An examination of Weismannism by George Romanes This idea was illuminated and explained by the rediscovery of Gregor Mendel's work in the early years of the 20th century (see Mendelian inheritance).
- [W10.67] Experiments on the inheritance of mutilation
- [W10.68] The idea that germline cells contain information that passes to each generation unaffected by experience and independent of the somatic (body) cells, came to be referred to as the Weismann barrier, and is frequently quoted as putting a final end to the theory of Lamarck and the inheritance of acquired characteristics.
- [W10.69] What Lamarck claimed was the inheritance of characteristics acquired through effort, or will.
- [W10.70] Weismann conducted the experiment of removing the tails of 68 white mice, repeatedly over 5 generations, and reporting that no mice were born in consequence without a tail or even with a shorter tail.
- [W10.71] He stated that "901 young were produced by five generations of artificially mutilated parents, and yet there was not a single example of a rudimentary tail or of any other abnormality in this organ." Weismann was aware of the limitations of this experiment, and made it clear that he embarked on the experiment precisely because, at the time, there were many claims of animals inheriting mutilations (he refers to a claim regarding a cat that had lost its tail having numerous tail-less offspring).
- [W10.72] There were also claims of Jews born without foreskins.
- [W10.73] None of these claims, he said, were backed up by reliable evidence that the parent had in fact been mutilated, leaving the perfectly plausible possibility that the modified offspring were the result of a mutated gene.
- [W10.74] The purpose of his experiment was to lay the claims of inherited mutilation to rest.
- [W10.75] The results were consistent with Weismann's germ plasm theory.
- [W10.76] Weismann was elected to honorary membership of the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1894.
- [W10.77] He was nominated the Honorary Fellow of the University of Tartu in 1902.
- [W10.78] He was elected an International Member of the American Philosophical Society in 1906.
- [W10.79] He was awarded the Linnean Society of London's Darwin-Wallace Medal in 1908.
- [W10.80] He was elected an International Member of the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1913.
- [W10.81] Ernst Mayr judged Weismann to be the most important evolutionary thinker between Darwin and the evolutionary synthesis around 1930–1940, and "one of the great biologists of all time".

## [W11] Wikipedia: Harriet Creighton
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harriet_Creighton&oldid=1348550548 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W11.1] Harriet Baldwin Creighton (June 27, 1909 – January 9, 2004) was an American botanist, geneticist and educator.
- [W11.2] She worked with Barbara McClintock on cytogenetics in the 1930s, and was elected president of the Botanical Society of America in 1956.
- [W11.3] Creighton was born in Delavan, Illinois, the daughter of Cyrus Murray Creighton and Bertha Baldwin Creighton.
- [W11.4] Her father was born in Canada.
- [W11.5] She graduated from Wellesley College in 1929, where she found botanist Margaret Clay Ferguson an encouraging faculty mentor.
- [W11.6] She completed her Ph.D. at Cornell University in 1933.
- [W11.7] At Cornell, she worked in the field of maize cytogenetics with Barbara McClintock.
- [W11.8] The pair published an influential paper in 1931, in which they described chromosomal crossover for the first time.
- [W11.9] This paper, part of her Ph.D. research, provided key evidence that chromosomes carried and exchanged genetic information and hence that genes for physical traits are carried on chromosomes.
- [W11.10] After completing her doctoral studies, Creighton taught at Cornell University and Connecticut College, and then returned to Wellesley College where she taught until her retirement in 1974.
- [W11.11] During World War II, she took leave from teaching to serve in the U.S.
- [W11.12] Creighton was elected in 1940 a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.
- [W11.13] In 1956 she was elected president of the Botanical Society of America.
- [W11.14] She held two Fulbright lectureships, which took her to the University of Western Australia in 1952, and to the Cusco, Peru, in 1959.
- [W11.15] "A Correlation of Cytological and Genetical Crossing-Over in Zea mays" (1931, with Barbara McClintock)
- [W11.16] "Three Cases of Deficiency in Chromosome 9 of Zea mays" (1934)

- [W11.23] Creighton's companion later in life was Gertrude Dever; they met in the WAVES and lived together for many years.
- [W11.24] Creighton died in 2004, at the age of 94, in Needham, Massachusetts.
- [W11.25] Wellesley College has a collection of her personal papers.
- [W11.26] Creighton's close personal and professional relationship with Barbara McClintock was dramatized in a 2023 play by Carolyn Gage, In McClintock's Corn.

## [W12] Wikipedia: Coefficient of relationship
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Coefficient_of_relationship&oldid=1283880980 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W12.1] The coefficient of relationship is a measure of the degree of consanguinity (or biological relationship) between two individuals.
- [W12.2] The term coefficient of relationship was defined by Sewall Wright in 1922, and was derived from his definition of the coefficient of inbreeding of 1921.
- [W12.3] The measure is most commonly used in genetics and genealogy.
- [W12.4] A coefficient of inbreeding can be calculated for an individual, and is typically one-half the coefficient of relationship between the parents.
- [W12.5] In general, the higher the level of inbreeding the closer the coefficient of relationship between the parents approaches a value of 1, expressed as a percentage, and approaches a value of 0 for individuals with arbitrarily remote common ancestors.
- [W12.6] Coefficient of relationship
- [W12.7] The coefficient of relationship
- [W12.8] between two people B and C is obtained by a summation of coefficients calculated for every line by which they are connected to their common ancestors.
- [W12.9] Each such line connects the two people via a common ancestor, passing through no person who is not a common ancestor more than once.
- [W12.10] A path coefficient between an ancestor A and an offspring O separated by
- [W12.11] {\displaystyle p_{AO}=2^{-n}\cdot {\sqrt {\frac {1+f_{A}}{1+f_{O}}}}}
- [W12.12] are the coefficients of inbreeding for A and O, respectively.
- [W12.13] The coefficient of relationship
- [W12.14] is now obtained by summing over all path coefficients:
- [W12.15] {\displaystyle r_{BC}=\sum p_{AB}\cdot p_{AC}}
- [W12.16] By assuming that the pedigree can be traced back to a sufficiently remote population of perfectly random-bred stock (fA = 0 for all A in the sum) the definition of r may be simplified to
- [W12.17] {\displaystyle r_{BC}=\sum _{p}2^{-L(p)}}
- [W12.18] where p enumerates all paths connecting B and C with unique common ancestors (i.e. all paths terminate at a common ancestor and may not pass through a common ancestor to a common ancestor's ancestor), and L(p) is the length of the path p.
- [W12.19] To give an (artificial) example:
- [W12.20] Assuming that two people share the same 32 ancestors of n = 5 generations ago, but do not have any common ancestors at four or fewer generations ago, their coefficient of relationship would be
- [W12.21] {\textstyle r=2^{n}\cdot 2^{-2n}=2^{-n}}
- [W12.22] {\textstyle 2^{-5}={\frac {1}{32}}}
- [W12.23] , equal to 0.03125 or approximately 3%.
- [W12.24] People for which the same situation applies for their 1024 ancestors of ten generations ago would have a coefficient of r =  2−10 = 0.1%.
- [W12.25] If follows that the value of r can be given to an accuracy of a few percent if the family tree of both people is known for a depth of five generations, and to an accuracy of a tenth of a percent if the known depth is at least ten generations.
- [W12.26] The contribution to r from common ancestors of 20 generations ago (corresponding to roughly 500 years in human genealogy, or the contribution from common descent from a medieval population) falls below one part-per-million.
- [W12.27] The coefficient of relationship is sometimes used to express degrees of kinship in numeric terms in human genealogy.
- [W12.28] In human relationships, the value of the coefficient of relationship is usually calculated based on the knowledge of a full family tree extending to a comparatively small number of generations, perhaps of the order of three or four.
- [W12.29] As explained above, the value for the coefficient of relationship so calculated is thus a lower bound, with an actual value that may be up to a few percent higher.
- [W12.30] The value is accurate to within 1% if the full family tree of both individuals is known to a depth of seven generations.
- [W12.31] A first-degree relative (FDR) is a person's parent (father or mother), sibling (brother or sister) or child (son or daughter).
- [W12.32] It constitutes a category of family members that largely overlaps with the term nuclear family, but without spouses.
- [W12.33] If the persons are related by blood, the first degree relatives share approximately 50% of their genes.
- [W12.34] First-degree relatives are a common measure used to diagnose risks for common diseases by analyzing family history.
- [W12.35] A second-degree relative (SDR) is someone who shares 25% of a person's genes.
- [W12.36] It includes uncles, aunts, nephews, nieces, grandparents, grandchildren, half-siblings and double-first cousins.
- [W12.37] Third-degree relatives are a segment of the extended family and includes first cousins, great-grandparents and great-grandchildren.
- [W12.38] Third-degree relatives are generally defined by the expected amount of genetic overlap that exists between two people, with the third-degree relatives of an individual sharing approximately 12.5% of their genes.
- [W12.39] The category includes great-grandparents, great-grandchildren, granduncles,  grandaunts, grandnephews, grandnieces, first cousins, half-uncles, half-aunts, half-nieces and half-nephews.
- [W12.40] In a clinical sense, marriage between two family members who have r = 3.125% (2−5) or higher qualifies as consanguineous marriage.
- [W12.41] Most incest laws concern the relationships where r = 25% (2−2) or higher, although many ignore the rare case of double first cousins.
- [W12.42] Some jurisdictions also prohibit sexual relations or marriage between cousins of various degree, or individuals related only through adoption or affinity.
- [W12.43] Whether there is any likelihood of conception is generally considered irrelevant.
- [W12.44] The kinship coefficient is a simple measure of relatedness, defined as the probability that a pair of randomly sampled homologous alleles are identical by descent.
- [W12.45] More simply, it is the probability that an allele selected randomly from an individual, i, and an allele selected at the same autosomal locus from another individual, j, are identical and from the same ancestor.
- [W12.46] The coefficient of relatedness is equal to twice the kinship coefficient.
- [W12.47] The kinship coefficient between two individuals, i and j, is represented as Φij.
- [W12.48] The kinship coefficient between a non-inbred individual and itself, Φii, is equal to 1/2.
- [W12.49] This is due to the fact that humans are diploid, meaning the only way for the randomly chosen alleles to be identical by descent is if the same allele is chosen twice (probability 1/2).
- [W12.50] Similarly, the relationship between a parent and a child is found by the chance that the randomly picked allele in the child is from the parent (probability 1/2) and the probability of the allele that is picked from the parent being the same one passed to the child (probability 1/2).
- [W12.51] Since these two events are independent of each other, they are multiplied Φij = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
- [W12.52] "Systems of Mating" (PDF).
- [W12.53] 6 (2): 111–178. doi:10.1093/genetics/6.2.111.
- [W12.54] PMID 17245958. five papers:
- [W12.55] I) The biometric relations between offspring and parent
- [W12.56] II) The effects of inbreeding on the genetic composition of a population
- [W12.57] III) Assortative mating based on somatic resemblance
- [W12.58] IV) The effects of selection
- [W12.59] "Coefficients of inbreeding and relationship".

- [W12.61] (1948) Les mathématiques de l'hérédité, Masson et Cie, Paris.
- [W12.62] (1997) Mathematical and statistical methods for genetic analysis, Springer-Verlag, New-York.
- [W12.63] M. van Arendonk; Piter Bijma (May 2006).
