## [W13] Wikipedia: Sibling
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sibling&oldid=1375378934 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W13.1] A sibling is a relative that shares at least one parent with the other person.
- [W13.2] A male sibling is a brother, and a female sibling is a sister.
- [W13.3] A person with no siblings is an only child.
- [W13.4] While some circumstances can cause siblings to be raised separately (such as foster care or adoption), most societies have siblings grow up together.
- [W13.5] This causes the development of strong emotional bonds, with siblinghood considered a unique type of relationship.
- [W13.6] The emotional bond between siblings is often complicated and is influenced by factors such as parental treatment, birth order, personality, and personal experiences outside the family.
- [W13.7] Medically, a full-sibling is a first-degree relative and a half-sibling is a second-degree relative as they are related by 50% and 25%, respectively.
- [W13.8] The word sibling was reintroduced in 1903 in an article in Biometrika, as a translation for the German Geschwister, having not been used since Middle English, specifically 1425.
- [W13.9] Siblings or full-siblings ([full] sisters or brothers) share the same biological parents.
- [W13.10] Full-siblings are also the most common type of siblings.
- [W13.11] Twins are siblings that are born from the same pregnancy.
- [W13.12] Twins generally share a greater bond due to growing up together and being the same age.
- [W13.13] Half-siblings (half-sisters or half-brothers) are people who share one parent.
- [W13.14] They may share the same mother but different fathers (in which case they are known as uterine siblings or maternal half-siblings), or they may have the same father but different mothers (in which case, they are known as agnate siblings or paternal half-siblings.
- [W13.15] In law, the term consanguine is used in place of agnate).
- [W13.16] In law (and especially inheritance law), half-siblings have often been accorded treatment unequal to that of full-siblings.
- [W13.17] Old English common law at one time incorporated inequalities into the laws of intestate succession, with half-siblings taking only half as much property of their intestate siblings' estates as siblings of full-blood.
- [W13.18] Unequal treatment of this type has been wholly abolished in England, but still exists in Florida.
- [W13.19] Three-quarter siblings share one parent, while the unshared parents are first-degree relatives to each other, for example, if a man has children with two women who are sisters, or a woman has children with a man and his son.
- [W13.20] In the first case, the children are half-siblings as well as first cousins; in the second, the children are half-siblings as well as a half-avuncular pair.
- [W13.21] They are genetically closer than half-siblings but less genetically close than full-siblings, a degree of genetic relationship that is rare in humans and little-studied.
- [W13.22] One notable example of three-quarter siblings is the family of American aviator Charles Lindbergh, who fathered children with two German sisters, Brigitte and Marietta Hesshaimer.
- [W13.23] Diblings, a portmanteau of donor sibling, or donor-conceived sibling, or donor-sperm sibling, are biologically connected through donated eggs or sperm.
- [W13.24] Diblings are biologically siblings though not legally for the purposes of family rights and inheritance.
- [W13.25] The anonymity of donation is seen to add complication to the process of courtship.
- [W13.26] Stepsiblings (stepbrothers or stepsisters) are the children of one's stepparent from a previous relationship.
- [W13.27] Adoptive siblings are raised by a person who is the adoptive parent of one and the adoptive or biological parent of the other.
- [W13.28] Siblings-in-law are the siblings of one's spouse, the spouse of one's sibling, or the spouse of one's spouse's sibling.
- [W13.29] The spouse of one's spouse's sibling may also be called a co-sibling.
- [W13.30] Foster siblings are children who are raised in the same foster home: foster children of one's parent(s), or the children or foster children of one's foster parent.
- [W13.31] God siblings are the children of the godfather or godmother or the godchildren of the father or mother.
- [W13.32] Milk siblings are children who have been nursed by the same woman.
- [W13.33] This relationship exists in cultures with milk kinship and in Islamic law.
- [W13.34] Cross-siblings are individuals who share one or more half-siblings; if one person has at least one maternal half-sibling and at least one paternal half-sibling, the maternal and paternal half-siblings are cross-siblings to each other.
- [W13.35] Consanguinity and genetics
- [W13.36] Consanguinity is the measure of how closely people are related.
- [W13.37] Genetic relatedness measures how many genes a person shares.
- [W13.38] As all humans share over 99% of the same genes, consanguinity only matters for the small fraction of genes which vary between different people.
- [W13.39] Inheritance of genes has a random element to it, and these two concepts are different.
- [W13.40] Consanguinity decreases by half for every generation of reproductive separation through their most recent common ancestor.
- [W13.41] Siblings are 50% related by consanguinity as they are separated from each other by two generation (sibling to parent to sibling), and they share two parents as common ancestors (
- [W13.42] {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {1}{2}}\right)^{2}+\left({\tfrac {1}{2}}\right)^{2}}
- [W13.43] A fraternal twin is a sibling and, therefore, is related by 50% consanguinity.
- [W13.44] Fraternal twins are no more genetically similar than regular siblings.
- [W13.45] As identical twins come from the same zygote, their most recent common ancestor is each other.
- [W13.46] They’re genetically identical and 100% consanguineous as they’re separated by zero generations (
- [W13.47] {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {1}{2}}\right)^{0}}
- [W13.48] Twin studies have been conducted by scientists to examine the roles that genetics and environment play in the development of various traits.
- [W13.49] Such studies examine how often identical twins possess the same behavioral trait and compare it to how often fraternal twins possess the same trait.
- [W13.50] In other studies twins are raised in separate families, and studies compare the passing on of a behavioral trait by the family environment and the possession of a common trait between identical twins.
- [W13.51] This kind of study has revealed that for personality traits which are known to be heritable, genetics play a substantial role throughout life and an even larger role during early years.
- [W13.52] Half-siblings are 25% related by consanguinity as they share one parent and separated from each other by two generations (
- [W13.53] {\displaystyle \left({\tfrac {1}{2}}\right)^{2}}
- [W13.54] A person may share more than the standard consanguinity with their sibling if their parents are closely biologically related (the coefficient of inbreeding is greater than zero).
- [W13.55] Interestingly, half-siblings can be related by as "three-quarters siblings" (related by 3/8) if their unshared parents have a consanguinity of 50%.
- [W13.56] This means the unshared parents are either siblings, making the half-siblings cousins, or parent and child, making them half- aunt-uncle and niece-nephew.
- [W13.57] In practice, full siblings do not share exactly 50% of their DNA, as chromosomal crossover only occurs a limited number of times and, therefore, large chunks of a chromosome are shared or not shared at one time.
- [W13.58] In fact, the mean DNA fraction shared is 50.28% with a standard deviation of 3.68%, meaning approximately 1/4 of sibling pairs share more than 52.76% of their DNA, while 1/4 share less than 47.8%.
- [W13.59] There is a very small chance that two half-siblings might not share any genes if they didn't inherit any of the same chromosomes from their shared parent.
- [W13.60] This is possible for full-siblings as well, though even more unlikely.
- [W13.61] But because of how homologous chromosomes swap genes (due to chromosomal crossover during meiosis) during the development of an egg or sperm cell, however, the odds of this ever actually occurring are practically non-existent.
- [W13.62] Birth order is a person's rank by age among their siblings.
- [W13.63] Typically, researchers classify siblings as "eldest", "middle child", and "youngest" or simply distinguish between "first-born" and "later-born" children.
- [W13.64] Birth order is commonly believed in pop psychology and popular culture to have a profound and lasting effect on psychological development and personality.
- [W13.65] For example, firstborns are seen as conservative and high-achieving, middle children as natural mediators, and youngest children as charming and outgoing.
- [W13.66] Despite its lasting presence in the public domain, studies have failed to consistently produce clear, valid, compelling findings; therefore, it has earned the title of a pseudo-psychology amongst the scientific psychological community.
- [W13.67] The theorizing and study of birth order can be traced back to Francis Galton's (1822–1911) theory of birth order and eminence and Alfred Adler's (1870–1937) theory of birth order and personality characteristics.
- [W13.68] In his book English Men of Science: Their Nature and Nurture (1874), Galton noted that prominent composers and scientists are over-represented as first-borns.
- [W13.69] He theorized three main reasons as to why first-borns are generally more eminent:
- [W13.70] Primogeniture laws: first-borns have access to their parents' financial resources to continue their education.
- [W13.71] First-borns are given more responsibility than their younger siblings and are treated more as companions by their parents.
- [W13.72] First-borns are given more attention and nourishment in families with limited financial resources.
- [W13.73] First Borns: Fulfilling family roles of leadership and authority, obedient of protocol and hierarchy.
- [W13.74] Seek out and prefer order, structure and adherence to norms and rules.
- [W13.75] They partake in goal-striving behaviour as their lives are centred around achievement and accomplishment themes.
- [W13.76] They fear the loss of their position in the top of the hierarchy.
- [W13.77] Middle Children: Feel like outcasts of families as they lack primacy of the first child and the "attention garnering recency" of the youngest.
- [W13.78] These children often go to great lengths to de-identify themselves with their siblings, in an attempt to make a different and individualized identity for themselves as they feel like they were "squeezed out" of their families.
- [W13.79] Youngest Children: Feel disadvantaged compared to older siblings, are often perceived as less capable or experienced and are therefore indulged and spoiled.
- [W13.80] Because of this, they are skilled in coaxing/charming others to do things for them or provide.
- [W13.81] This contributes to the image of them being popular and outgoing, as they engage in attention-seeking behaviour to meet their needs.
- [W13.82] The flaws and inconsistencies in birth order research eliminate its validity.
- [W13.83] It is very difficult to control solely for factors related to birth order, and therefore most studies produce ambiguous results.
- [W13.84] Embedded into theories of birth order is a debate of nature versus nurture.
- [W13.85] It has been disproved that there is something innate in the position one is born into, and therefore creating a preset role.
- [W13.86] Birth order has no genetic basis.
- [W13.87] The social interaction that occurs as a result of birth order however is the most notable.
- [W13.88] Older siblings often become role models of behaviour, and younger siblings become learners and supervisees.
- [W13.89] Older siblings are at a developmental advantage both cognitively and socially.
- [W13.90] The role of birth order also depends greatly and varies greatly on family context.
- [W13.91] Family size, sibling identification, age gap, modeling, parenting techniques, gender, class, race, and temperament are all confounding variables that can influence behaviour and therefore perceived behaviour of specific birth categories.
- [W13.92] The research on birth order does have stronger correlations, however, in areas such as intelligence and physical features, but are likely caused by other factors other than the actual position of birth.
- [W13.93] Some research has found that firstborn children have slightly higher IQs on average than later born children.
- [W13.94] However, other research finds no such effect.
- [W13.95] It has been found that first-borns score three points higher compared to second borns and that children born earlier in a family are on average, taller and weigh more than those born later.
- [W13.96] However, it is impossible to generalize birth order characteristics and apply them universally to all individuals in that subgroup.
- [W13.97] Contemporary explanations for IQ findings
- [W13.98] (Blake, 1981) provide three potential reasons for the higher scoring of older siblings on IQ tests:
- [W13.99] Parental resources are finite, first-born children get full and primary access to these resources.
- [W13.100] As the number of a children in a family goes up, the more resources must be shared.
- [W13.101] These parental resources have an important impact on a child's educational success.
- [W13.102] Robert Zajonc proposed that the intellectual environment within a family is ever-changing due to three factors, and therefore more permissive of first-born children's intellectual advancement:
- [W13.103] Firstborns do not need to share parental attention and have their parents' complete absorption.
- [W13.104] More siblings in the family limit the attention devoted to each of them.
- [W13.105] Firstborns are exposed to more adult language.
- [W13.106] Later-borns are exposed to the less-mature speech of their older siblings.
- [W13.107] Firstborns and older siblings must answer questions and explain things to younger siblings, acting as tutors.
- [W13.108] This advances their cognitive processing of information and language skills.
- [W13.109] In 1996, interest in the science behind birth order was re-sparked when Frank Sulloway’s book Born To Rebel was published.
- [W13.110] In this book, Sulloway argues that firstborns are more conscientious, more socially dominant, less agreeable, and less open to new ideas compared to later-borns.
- [W13.111] While being seemingly empirical and academic, as many studies are cited throughout the book, it is still often criticized as a biased and incomplete account of the whole picture of siblings and birth order.
- [W13.112] Because it is a novel, the research and theories proposed throughout were not criticized and peer-reviewed by other academics before its release.
- [W13.113] Literature reviews that have examined many studies and attempted to control for confounding variables tend to find minimal effects for birth order on personality.
- [W13.114] In her review of the scientific literature, Judith Rich Harris suggests that birth order effects may exist within the context of the family of origin, but that they are not enduring aspects of personality.
- [W13.115] In practice, systematic birth order research is a challenge because it is difficult to control for all of the variables that are statistically related to birth order.
- [W13.116] For example, large families are generally lower in socioeconomic status than small families, so third-born children are more likely than first-born children to come from poorer families.
- [W13.117] Spacing of children, parenting style, and gender are additional variables to consider.
- [W13.118] Regressive behavior at birth
- [W13.119] Regressive behaviors are the child's way of demanding the parents' love and attention.
- [W13.120] The arrival of a new baby is especially stressful for firstborns and for siblings between 3 and 5 years old.
- [W13.121] In such situations, regressive behavior may be accompanied by aggressive behavior, such as handling the baby roughly.
- [W13.122] All of these symptoms are considered to be typical and developmentally appropriate for children between the ages of 3 and 5.
- [W13.123] While some can be prevented, the remainder can be improved within a few months.
- [W13.124] Regressive behavior may include demand for a bottle, thumb sucking, requests to wear diapers (even if toilet-trained), or requests to carry a security blanket.
- [W13.125] The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests that instead of protesting or telling children to act their age, parents should simply grant their requests without becoming upset.
- [W13.126] The affected children will soon return to their normal routine when they realize that they now have just as important a place in the family as the new sibling.
- [W13.127] Most of the behaviors can be improved within a few months.
- [W13.128] The University of Michigan Health System advises that most occurrences of regressive behavior are mild and to be expected; however, it recommends parents to contact a pediatrician or child psychologist if the older child tries to hurt the baby, if regressive behavior does not improve within 2 or 3 months, or if the parents have other questions or concerns.
- [W13.129] "Sibling rivalry" is a type of competition or animosity among brothers and sisters.
- [W13.130] It appears to be particularly intense when children are very close in age or of the same gender.
- [W13.131] Sibling rivalry can involve aggression; however, it is not the same as sibling abuse where one child victimizes another.
- [W13.132] Sibling rivalry usually starts right after, or before, the arrival of the second child.
- [W13.133] While siblings will still love each other, it is not uncommon for them to bicker and be malicious to each other.
- [W13.134] Children are sensitive from the age of 1 year to differences in parental treatment and by 3 years they have a sophisticated grasp of family rules and can evaluate themselves in relation to their siblings.
- [W13.135] Sibling rivalry often continues throughout childhood and can be very frustrating and stressful to parents.
- [W13.136] One study found that the age group 10–15 reported the highest level of competition between siblings.
- [W13.137] This competition can also cause behavioral spillover where siblings, intentionally or not, influence each other's life trajectories in a positive manner as they attempt to differentiate and challenge themselves to excel, vying for their parents' praise.
- [W13.138] Sibling rivalry can continue into adulthood and sibling relationships can change dramatically over the years.
- [W13.139] Approximately one-third of adults describe their relationship with siblings as rivalrous or distant.
- [W13.140] However, rivalry often lessens over time and at least 80% of siblings over age 60 enjoy close ties.
- [W13.141] Each child in a family competes to define who they are as persons and want to show that they are separate from their siblings.
- [W13.142] Sibling rivalry increases when children feel they are getting unequal amounts of their parents' attention, where there is stress in the parents' and children's lives, and where fighting is accepted by the family as a way to resolve conflicts.
- [W13.143] Sigmund Freud saw the sibling relationship as an extension of the Oedipus complex, where brothers were in competition for their mother's attention and sisters for their father's.
- [W13.144] Evolutionary psychologists explain sibling rivalry in terms of parental investment and kin selection: a parent is inclined to spread resources equally among all children in the family, but a child wants most of the resources for him or herself.
- [W13.145] Jealousy is not a single emotion.
- [W13.146] The basic emotions expressed in jealous interactions are fear, anger, relief, sadness, and anxiety.
- [W13.147] Jealousy occurs in a social triangle of relationships which do not require a third person.
- [W13.148] The social triangle involves the relationships between the jealous individual and the parent, the relationship between the parent and the rival, and the relationship between jealous individual and the rival.
- [W13.149] First-borns' attachment to their parents is directly related to their jealous behaviour.
- [W13.150] In a study by Volling, four classes of children were identified based on their different responses of jealousy to new infant siblings and parent interactions.
- [W13.151] Regulated Exploration Children: 60% of children fall into this category.
- [W13.152] These children closely watch their parents interact with their newborn sibling, approach them positively and sometimes join the interaction.
- [W13.153] They show fewer behaviour problems in the months following the new birth and do not display problematic behaviours during the parent-infant interaction.
- [W13.154] These children are considered secure as they act how a child would be expected to act in a familiar home setting with their parents present as secure bases to explore the environment.
- [W13.155] Approach-Avoidant Children: 30% of children fall into this category.
- [W13.156] These children observe parent-infant interaction closely and are less likely to approach the infant and the parent.
- [W13.157] They are anxious to explore the new environment as they tend to seek little comfort from their parents.
- [W13.158] Anxious-Clingy Children:  6% of children fell into this category.
- [W13.159] These children have an intense interest in parent-infant interaction and a strong desire to seek proximity and contact with the parent, and sometimes intrude on parent-child interaction.
- [W13.160] Disruptive Children: 2.7% of children fall into this category.
- [W13.161] These children are emotionally reactive and aggressive.
- [W13.162] They have difficulty regulating their negative emotions and may be likely to externalize it as negative behaviour around the newborn.
- [W13.163] Children are more jealous of the interactions between newborns and their mothers than they are with newborns and their fathers.
- [W13.164] This is logical as up until the birth of the infant, the first-born child had the mother as their primary care-giver all to themselves.
- [W13.165] Some research has suggested that children display less jealous reactions over father-newborn interactions because fathers tend to punish negative emotion and are less tolerant than mothers of clinginess and visible distress, although this is hard to generalize.
- [W13.166] Children that have parents with a better marital relationship are better at regulating their jealous emotions.
- [W13.167] Children are more likely to express jealousy when their parents are directing their attention to the sibling as opposed to when the parents are solely interacting with them.
- [W13.168] Parents who are involved in good marital communication help their children cope adaptively with jealousy.
- [W13.169] They do this by modelling problem-solving and conflict resolution for their children.
- [W13.170] Children are also less likely to have jealous feelings when they live in a home in which everyone in the family shares and expresses love and happiness.
- [W13.171] Implicit theories about relationships are associated with the ways children think of strategies to deal with a new situation.
- [W13.172] Children can fall into two categories of implicit theorizing.
- [W13.173] They may be malleable theorists and believe that they can affect change on situations and people.
- [W13.174] Alternatively, they may be fixed theorists, believing situations and people are not changeable.
- [W13.175] These implicit beliefs determine both the intensity of their jealous feelings, and how long those jealous feelings last.
- [W13.176] Malleable Theorists display engaging behaviours, like interacting with the parent or sibling in an attempt to improve the situation.
- [W13.177] They tend to have more intense and longer-lasting feelings of jealousy because they spend more time ruminating on the situation and constructing ways to make it better.
- [W13.178] Fixed Theorists display non-engaging behaviours, for example retreating to their room because they believe none of their actions will affect or improve the situation.
- [W13.179] They tend to have less intense and shorter lasting feelings of jealousy than malleable theorists.
- [W13.180] Older children tend to be less jealous than their younger sibling.
- [W13.181] This is due to their ability to mentally process the social situation in a way that gives them more positive, empathetic feelings toward their younger sibling.
- [W13.182] Older children are better able to cope with their jealous feelings toward their younger sibling due to their understanding of the necessary relationship between the parent and younger sibling.
- [W13.183] Older children are also better at self-regulating their emotions and are less dependent on their caregivers for external regulation as opposed to their younger siblings.
- [W13.184] Younger siblings' feelings of jealousy are overpowered by feelings of anger.
- [W13.185] The quality of the relationship between the younger child and the older child is also a factor in jealousy, as the better the relationship the less jealous feelings occurred and vice versa.
- [W13.186] Sibling conflict is pervasive and often shrugged off as an accepted part of sibling dynamics.
- [W13.187] In spite of the broad variety of conflict that siblings are often involved in, sibling conflicts can be grouped into two broader categories.
- [W13.188] The first category is conflict about equality or fairness.
- [W13.189] It is not uncommon to see siblings who think that their sibling is favored by their teachers, peers, or especially their parents.
- [W13.190] In fact it is not uncommon to see siblings who both think that their parents favor the other sibling.
- [W13.191] Perceived inequalities in the division of resources such as who got a larger dessert also fall into this category of conflict.
- [W13.192] This form of conflict seems to be more prevalent in the younger sibling.
- [W13.193] The second category of conflict involves an invasion of a child's perceived personal domain by their sibling.
- [W13.194] An example of this type of conflict is when a child enters their sibling's room when they are not welcome, or when a child crosses over into their sibling's side of the car in a long road trip.
- [W13.195] These types of fights seem to be more important to older siblings due to their larger desire for independence.
- [W13.196] Sibling warmth is a term for the degree of affection and companionship shared by siblings.
- [W13.197] Sibling warmth seems to have an effect on siblings.
- [W13.198] Higher sibling warmth is related to better social skill and higher perceived social competence.
- [W13.199] Even in cases where there is a high level of sibling conflict if there is also a high level of sibling warmth then social skills and competence remain unaffected.
- [W13.200] Negative effects of conflict
- [W13.201] The saying that people "fight like siblings" shows just how charged sibling conflict can be and how well recognized sibling squabbles are.
- [W13.202] In spite of how widely acknowledged these squabbles can be, sibling conflict can have several impacts on the sibling pair.
- [W13.203] It has been shown that increased levels of sibling conflict are related to higher levels of anxiety and depression in siblings, along with lower levels of self-worth and lower levels of academic competence.
- [W13.204] In addition, sibling warmth is not a protective factor for the negative effects of anxiety, depression, lack of self-worth and lower levels of academic competence.
- [W13.205] This means that sibling warmth does not counteract these negative effects.
- [W13.206] Sibling conflict is also linked to an increase in more risky behavior including: smoking cigarettes, skipping days of school, contact with the police, and other behaviors in Caucasian sibling pairs with the exception of firstborns with younger brothers.
- [W13.207] Except for the elder brother in this pair sibling conflict is positively correlated with risky behavior, thus sibling conflict may be a risk factor for behavioral problems.
- [W13.208] A study on what the topic of the fight was (invasion of personal domain or inequality) also shows that the topic of the fight may have a result on the effects of the conflict.
- [W13.209] This study showed that sibling conflict over personal domain were related to lower levels of self-esteem, and sibling conflict over perceived inequalities seem to be more related to depressive symptoms.
- [W13.210] However, the study also showed that greater depressive and anxious symptoms were also related to more frequent sibling conflict and more intense sibling conflict.
- [W13.211] Parental management techniques of conflict
- [W13.212] Techniques used by parents to manage their children's conflicts include parental non-intervention, child-centered parental intervention strategies, and more rarely the encouragement of physical conflict between siblings.
- [W13.213] Parental non-intervention included techniques in which the parent ignores the siblings' conflict and lets them work it out between themselves without outside guidance.
- [W13.214] In some cases, this technique is chosen to avoid situations in which the parent decides which sibling is in the right and may favor one sibling over the other, however, by following this technique the parent may sacrifice the opportunity to instruct their children on how to deal with conflict.
- [W13.215] Child-centered parental interventions include techniques in which the parent mediates the argument between the two children and helps them come to an agreement.
- [W13.216] Using this technique, parents may help model how the children can deal with conflicts in the future; however, parents should avoid dictating the outcome to the children, and make sure that they are mediating the argument making suggestions, allowing the children to decide the outcome.
- [W13.217] This may be especially important when some of the children have autism.
- [W13.218] Techniques in which parents encourage physical aggression between siblings may be chosen by the parents to help children deal with aggression in the future, however, this technique does not appear to be effective as it is linked to greater conflict levels between children.
- [W13.219] Parental non-intervention is also linked to higher levels of sibling conflict, and lower levels of sibling warmth.
- [W13.220] It appears that child-centered parental interventions have the best effect on sibling's relationship with a link to greater levels of sibling warmth and lower levels of sibling conflict.
- [W13.221] Long-term effects of presence
- [W13.222] Studies on social skill and personality differences between only children and children with siblings suggest that overall the presence of a sibling does not have any effect on the child as an adult.
- [W13.223] However, working-class families who do not have the income for their children to participate in extracurricular activities such as sports or academia can benefit culturally and intellectually from the increased time those siblings spend together.
- [W13.224] Gender roles among children and parents
- [W13.225] There have always been some differences between siblings, especially different sex siblings.
- [W13.226] Often, different sex sibling may consider things to be unfair because their brother or sister is allowed to do certain things because of their gender, while they get to do something less fun or just different.
- [W13.227] McHale and her colleague conducted a longitudinal study using middle-childhood aged children and observed the way in which the parents contributed to stereotypical attitudes in their kids.
- [W13.228] In their study the experimenters analysed two different types of families, one with the same sex siblings, and the other with different sex siblings, as well as the children's birth order.
- [W13.229] The experiment was conducted using phone interviews, in which the experimenters would ask the children about the activities they performed throughout their day outside of school.
- [W13.230] The experimenters found that in the homes where there were mixed gender kids, and the father held traditional values, the kids also held traditional values and therefore also played gender based roles in the home.
- [W13.231] In contrast, in homes where the father did not hold traditional values, the house chores were divided more equally among his kids.
- [W13.232] However, if fathers had two male children, the younger male tended to help more with household chores, but as he reached his teenage years the younger child stopped being as helpful around the house.
- [W13.233] However, education may be a confounder affecting both the father's attitude and the siblings' behavior, and the mother's attitudes did not have a noticeable impact.
- [W13.234] Anthropologist Edvard Westermarck found that children who are brought up together as siblings are desensitized to sexual attraction to one another later in life.
- [W13.235] This is known as the Westermarck Effect.
- [W13.236] It can be seen in biological and adoptive families, but also in other situations where children are brought up in close contact, such as the Israeli kibbutz system and the Chinese shim-pua marriage.
- [W13.237] The Sibling Effect: What the Bonds Among Brothers and Sisters Reveal About Us.
- [W13.238] Media related to Siblings at Wikimedia Commons
- [W13.239] Cambridge University Press. p.
- [W13.240] Cambridge University Press. p.

## [W14] Wikipedia: Twin
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Twin&oldid=1381510781 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W14.1] Twins are two offspring produced by the same pregnancy.
- [W14.2] Twins can be either monozygotic ('identical'), meaning that they develop from one zygote, which splits and forms two embryos, or dizygotic ('non-identical' or 'fraternal'), meaning that each twin develops from a separate egg and each egg is fertilized by its own sperm cell.
- [W14.3] Since identical twins develop from one zygote, they will share the same chromosomal sex, while fraternal twins may or may not.
- [W14.4] In very rare cases, fraternal or (semi-) identical twins can have the same mother and different fathers.
- [W14.5] In contrast, a fetus that develops alone in the womb (the much more common case in humans) is a singleton; one of a multiple birth is a multiple.
- [W14.6] Unrelated look-alikes whose resemblance parallels that of twins are referred to as doppelgänger.
- [W14.7] The human twin birth rate in the United States rose 76% from 1980 through 2009, from 9.4 to 16.7 twin sets (18.8 to 33.3 twins) per 1,000 births.
- [W14.8] The Yoruba people have the highest rate of twinning in the world, at 45–50 twin sets (90–100 twins) per 1,000 live births, possibly because of high consumption of a specific type of yam containing a natural phytoestrogen which may stimulate the ovaries to release an egg from each side.
- [W14.9] In Central Africa, there are 18–30 twin sets (or 36–60 twins) per 1,000 live births.
- [W14.10] In South America, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, the lowest rates are found: only six to nine twin sets per thousand live births.
- [W14.11] North America and Europe have intermediate rates of nine to sixteen twin sets per thousand live births.
- [W14.12] In the United Kingdom, approximately one in 65 pregnancies results in a multiple birth.
- [W14.13] There has been an upward trend in the number of multiple births, which is attributed to various factors including fertility treatments,  the survival rates of premature babies and women delaying starting their families.
- [W14.14] Multiple pregnancies are much less likely to carry to full term than single births, with twin pregnancies lasting on average 37 weeks, three weeks less than full term.
- [W14.15] Women who have a family history of fraternal twins have a higher chance of producing fraternal twins themselves, as there is a genetically linked tendency to hyper-ovulate.
- [W14.16] There is no known genetic link for identical twinning.
- [W14.17] Other factors that increase the odds of having fraternal twins include maternal age, fertility drugs and other fertility treatments, nutrition, and prior births.
- [W14.18] Some women intentionally turn to fertility drugs in order to conceive twins.\
- [W14.19] Dizygotic (fraternal) twins
- [W14.20] Dizygotic (DZ) or fraternal twins (also referred to as non-identical twins, dissimilar twins, biovular twins, and, informally in the case of females, sororal twins) usually occur when two fertilized eggs are implanted in the uterus wall at the same time.
- [W14.21] When two eggs are independently fertilized by two different sperm cells, fraternal twins result.
- [W14.22] The two eggs, or ova, form two zygotes, hence the terms dizygotic and biovular.
- [W14.23] Fraternal twins are, essentially, two ordinary siblings who happen to develop in the womb together and who are born at the same time, since they arise from two separate eggs fertilized by two separate sperm, just like ordinary siblings.
- [W14.24] This is the most common type of twin.
- [W14.25] Dizygotic twins, like any other siblings, will practically always have different sequences on each chromosome, due to chromosomal crossover during meiosis.
- [W14.26] Dizygotic twins share on average 50 percent of each other's genes, the same as siblings that are conceived and born at different times.
- [W14.27] Like any other siblings, dizygotic twins may look similar, particularly as they are the same age.
- [W14.28] However, dizygotic twins may also look very different from each other (for example, be of opposite sexes).
- [W14.29] Studies show that there is a genetic proclivity for dizygotic twinning.
- [W14.30] However, it is only the mother who has any effect on the chances of having such twins; there is no known mechanism for a father to cause the release of more than one ovum.
- [W14.31] Dizygotic twinning ranges from six per thousand births in Japan (similar to the rate of monozygotic twins) to 14 and more per thousand in some African countries.
- [W14.32] Dizygotic twins are also more common for older mothers, with twinning rates doubling in mothers over the age of 35.
- [W14.33] With the advent of technologies and techniques to assist women in getting pregnant, the rate of fraternals has increased markedly.
- [W14.34] Monozygotic (identical) twins
- [W14.35] Monozygotic (MZ) or identical twins occur when a single egg is fertilized to form one zygote (hence, monozygotic) which then divides into two separate embryos.
- [W14.36] Regarding spontaneous or natural monozygotic twinning, a 2007 theory related to in vitro fertilization (IVF) proposes that monozygotic twins may be formed when a blastocyst contains two inner cell masses (ICM), each of which will lead to a separate fetus, rather than by the embryo splitting while hatching from the zona pellucida (the gelatinous protective coating around the blastocyst).
- [W14.37] Monozygotic twins may also be created artificially by embryo splitting.
- [W14.38] It can be used as an expansion of in vitro fertilization (IVF) to increase the number of available embryos for embryo transfer.
- [W14.39] The chance of identical twins is approximately 3 to 4 in every 1,000 births.
- [W14.40] The likelihood of a single fertilization resulting in monozygotic twins is uniformly distributed in all populations around the world.
- [W14.41] This is in marked contrast to dizygotic twinning, which ranges from about six per thousand births in Japan (almost similar to the rate of identical twins, which is around 4–5) to 15 and more per thousand in some parts of India and up to over 20 in some Central African countries.
- [W14.42] The exact cause for the splitting of a zygote or embryo is unknown.
- [W14.43] IVF techniques are more likely to create dizygotic twins.
- [W14.44] For IVF deliveries, there are nearly 21 pairs of twins for every 1,000.
- [W14.45] Genetic and epigenetic similarity
- [W14.46] Monozygotic twins are genetically nearly identical and they are the same chromosomal sex unless there has been a mutation during development.
- [W14.47] The children of monozygotic twins test genetically as half-siblings (or full siblings, if a pair of monozygotic twins reproduces with another pair or with the same person), rather than first cousins.
- [W14.48] Identical twins do not have the same fingerprints however, because even within the confines of the womb, the fetuses touch different parts of their environment, giving rise to small variations in their corresponding prints and thus making them unique.
- [W14.49] Monozygotic twins can have rare differences in their genotypes, normally due to an environmental factor or the deactivation of different X chromosomes in female monozygotic twins.
- [W14.50] In some extremely rare cases, due to aneuploidy, twins may express different sexual phenotypes, typically from an XXY Klinefelter syndrome zygote splitting unevenly.
- [W14.51] To quantify the occurrence of such genotypic differences, a 2013 study of DNA in white blood cells of 66 pairs of monozygotic twins tested for 506,786 single-nucleotide polymorphisms known to occur in human populations.
- [W14.52] Polymorphisms appeared in 2 of the 33 million comparisons, leading the researchers to extrapolate that the blood cells of monozygotic twins may have on the order of one DNA-sequence difference for every 12 million nucleotides, which would imply hundreds of differences across the entire genome.
- [W14.53] The mutations producing the differences detected in this study would have occurred during embryonic cell-division (after the point of fertilization).
- [W14.54] If they occur early in fetal development, they will be present in a very large proportion of body cells.
- [W14.55] Another cause of difference between monozygotic twins is epigenetic modification, caused by differing environmental influences throughout their lives.
- [W14.56] Epigenetics refers to the level of activity of any particular gene.
- [W14.57] A gene may become switched on, switched off, or could become partially switched on or off in an individual.
- [W14.58] This epigenetic modification is triggered by environmental events.
- [W14.59] Monozygotic twins can have markedly different epigenetic profiles.
- [W14.60] A study of 80 pairs of monozygotic twins ranging in age from three to 74 showed that the youngest twins have relatively few epigenetic differences.
- [W14.61] The number of epigenetic differences increases with age.
- [W14.62] Fifty-year-old twins had over three times the epigenetic difference of three-year-old twins.
- [W14.63] Twins who had spent their lives apart (such as those adopted by two different sets of parents at birth) had the greatest difference.
- [W14.64] However, certain characteristics become more alike as twins age, such as IQ and personality.
- [W14.65] A four-year study of monozygotic twins and their extended families, published in Nature Genetics in 2021, found that these twins have genetic differences that begin in the early stages of embryonic development.
- [W14.66] Polar body and semi-identical twins
- [W14.67] A 1981 study of a deceased XXX twin fetus without a heart showed that although its fetal development suggested that it was an identical twin, as it shared a placenta with its healthy twin, tests revealed that it was probably a polar body twin.
- [W14.68] The authors were unable to predict whether a healthy fetus could result from a polar body twinning.
- [W14.69] However, a study in 2012 found that it is possible for a polar body to result in a healthy fetus.
- [W14.70] In 2003, a study argued that many cases of triploidy arise from sesquizygotic (semi-identical) twinning which happens when a single egg is fertilized by two sperm and splits the three sets of chromosomes into two separate cell sets.
- [W14.71] The degree of separation of the twins in utero depends on if and when they split into two zygotes.
- [W14.72] Dizygotic twins were always two zygotes.
- [W14.73] Monozygotic twins split into two zygotes at some time very early in the pregnancy.
- [W14.74] The timing of this separation determines the chorionicity (the number of placentae) and amniocity (the number of sacs) of the pregnancy.
- [W14.75] Dichorionic twins either never divided (i.e.: were dizygotic) or they divided within the first four days.
- [W14.76] Monoamnionic twins divide after the first week.
- [W14.77] In very rare cases, twins become conjoined twins.
- [W14.78] Non-conjoined monozygotic twins form up to day 14 of embryonic development, but when twinning occurs after 14 days, the twins will likely be conjoined.
- [W14.79] Furthermore, there can be various degrees of shared environment of twins in the womb, potentially leading to pregnancy complications.
- [W14.80] It is a common misconception that two placentas automatically implies dizygotic twins, but if monozygotic twins separate early enough, the arrangement of sacs and placentas in utero is in fact indistinguishable from that of dizygotic twins.
- [W14.81] A 2006 study has found that insulin-like growth factor present in dairy products may increase the chance of dizygotic twinning.
- [W14.82] Specifically, the study found that vegan mothers (who exclude dairy from their diets) are one-fifth as likely to have twins as vegetarian or omnivore mothers, and concluded that "Genotypes favoring elevated IGF and diets including dairy products, especially in areas where growth hormone is given to cattle, appear to enhance the chances of multiple pregnancies due to ovarian stimulation."
- [W14.83] From 1980 to 1997, the number of twin births in the United States rose 52%.
- [W14.84] This rise can at least partly be attributed to the increasing popularity of fertility drugs and procedures such as IVF, which result in multiple births more frequently than unassisted fertilizations do.
- [W14.85] It may also be linked to the increase of growth hormones in food.
- [W14.86] About 1 in 90 human births (1.1%) results from a twin pregnancy.
- [W14.87] The rate of dizygotic twinning varies greatly among ethnic groups, ranging as high as about 45 per 1000 births (4.5%) for the Yoruba to 10% for Linha São Pedro, a tiny Brazilian settlement which belongs to the city of Cândido Godói.
- [W14.88] In Cândido Godói, one in five pregnancies has resulted in twins.
- [W14.89] The Argentine historian Jorge Camarasa has put forward the theory that experiments of the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele could be responsible for the high ratio of twins in the area.
- [W14.90] His theory was rejected by Brazilian scientists who had studied twins living in Linha São Pedro; they suggested genetic factors within that community as a more likely explanation.
- [W14.91] A high twinning rate has also been observed in other places of the world, including:
- [W14.92] Kodinhi, located in Kerala, India
- [W14.93] Mohammadpur Umri, located in Uttar Pradesh, India
- [W14.94] In a study on the maternity records of 5750 Hausa women living in the Savannah zone of Nigeria, there were 40 twins and 2 triplets per 1000 births.
- [W14.95] Twenty-six percent of twins were monozygotic.
- [W14.96] The incidence of multiple births, which was about five times higher than that observed in any western population, was significantly lower than that of other ethnic groups, who live in the hot and humid climate of the southern part of the country.
- [W14.97] The incidence of multiple births was related to maternal age but did not bear any association to the climate or prevalence of malaria.
- [W14.98] Twins are more common in people of African descent.
- [W14.99] The predisposing factors of monozygotic twinning are unknown.
- [W14.100] Dizygotic twin pregnancies are slightly more likely when the following factors are present in the woman:
- [W14.101] She is of West African descent (especially Yoruba)
- [W14.102] She is between the age of 30 and 40 years
- [W14.103] She is greater than average height and weight
- [W14.104] She has had several previous pregnancies.
- [W14.105] Women undergoing certain fertility treatments may have a greater chance of dizygotic multiple births.
- [W14.106] In the United States it has been estimated that by 2011 36% of twin births resulted from conception by assisted reproductive technology.
- [W14.107] The risk of twin birth can vary depending on what types of fertility treatments are used.
- [W14.108] With in vitro fertilisation (IVF), this is primarily due to the insertion of multiple embryos into the uterus.
- [W14.109] Ovarian hyperstimulation without IVF has a very high risk of multiple birth.
- [W14.110] Reversal of anovulation with clomifene (trade names including Clomid) has a relatively less but yet significant risk of multiple pregnancy.
- [W14.111] A 15-year German study of 8,220 vaginally delivered twins (that is, 4,110 pregnancies) in Hesse yielded a mean delivery time interval of 13.5 minutes.
- [W14.112] The delivery interval between the twins was measured as follows:
- [W14.113] The study stated that the occurrence of complications "was found to be more likely with increasing twin-to-twin delivery time interval" and suggested that the interval be kept short, though it noted that the study did not examine causes of complications and did not control for factors such as the level of experience of the obstetrician, the wish of the women giving birth, or the "management strategies" of the procedure of delivering the second twin.
- [W14.114] There have also been cases in which twins are born a number of days apart.
- [W14.115] Possibly the worldwide record for the duration of the time gap between the first and the second delivery was the birth of twins 97 days apart in Cologne, Germany, the first of which was born on November 17, 2018.
- [W14.116] Complications during pregnancy
- [W14.117] Researchers suspect that as many as 1 in 8 pregnancies start out as multiples, but only a single fetus is brought to full term, because the other fetus has died very early in the pregnancy and has not been detected or recorded.
- [W14.118] Early obstetric ultrasonography exams sometimes reveal an "extra" fetus, which fails to develop and instead disintegrates and vanishes in the uterus.
- [W14.119] There are several reasons for the "vanishing" fetus, including it being embodied or absorbed by the other fetus, placenta or the mother.
- [W14.120] This is known as vanishing twin syndrome.
- [W14.121] Also, in an unknown proportion of cases, two zygotes may fuse soon after fertilization, resulting in a single chimeric embryo, and, later, fetus.
- [W14.122] Conjoined twins (or the once-commonly used term Siamese) are monozygotic twins whose bodies are joined during pregnancy.
- [W14.123] This occurs when the zygote starts to split after day 12 following fertilization and fails to separate completely.
- [W14.124] This condition occurs in about 1 in 50,000 human pregnancies.
- [W14.125] Most conjoined twins are now evaluated for surgery to attempt to separate them into separate functional bodies.
- [W14.126] The degree of difficulty rises if a vital organ or structure is shared between twins, such as the brain, heart, liver or lungs.
- [W14.127] A chimera is an ordinary person or animal except that some of their parts actually came from their twin or from the mother.
- [W14.128] A chimera may arise either from monozygotic twin fetuses (where it would be impossible to detect), or from dizygotic fetuses, which can be identified by chromosomal comparisons from various parts of the body.
- [W14.129] The number of cells derived from each fetus can vary from one part of the body to another, and often leads to characteristic mosaicism skin coloration in human chimeras.
- [W14.130] In one case DNA tests falsely determined that a woman, Lydia Fairchild, mystifyingly, was not the mother of two of her three children; she was found to be a chimera, and the two children were conceived from eggs derived from cells of their mother's twin.
- [W14.131] Sometimes one twin fetus will fail to develop completely and continue to cause problems for its surviving twin.
- [W14.132] One fetus acts as a parasite towards the other.
- [W14.133] Sometimes the parasitic twin becomes an almost indistinguishable part of the other, and sometimes this needs to be treated medically.
- [W14.134] A very rare type of parasitic twinning is one where a single viable twin is endangered when the other zygote becomes cancerous, or molar.
- [W14.135] This means that the molar zygote's cellular division continues unchecked, resulting in a cancerous growth that overtakes the viable fetus.
- [W14.136] Typically, this results when one twin has either triploidy or complete paternal uniparental disomy, resulting in little or no fetus and a cancerous, overgrown placenta, resembling a bunch of grapes.
- [W14.137] Occasionally, a woman will suffer a miscarriage early in pregnancy, yet the pregnancy will continue; one twin was miscarried but the other was able to be carried to term.
- [W14.138] This occurrence is similar to the vanishing twin syndrome, but typically occurs later, as the twin is not reabsorbed.
- [W14.139] It is very common for twins to be born at a low birth weight.
- [W14.140] More than half of twins are born weighing less than 5.5 pounds (2.5 kg), while the average birth weight of a healthy baby should be around 6–8 pounds (3–4 kg).
- [W14.141] This is largely due to the fact that twins are typically born premature.
- [W14.142] Premature birth and low birth weights, especially when under 3.5 pounds (1.6 kg), can increase the risk of several health-related issues, such as vision and hearing loss, mental disabilities, and cerebral palsy.
- [W14.143] There is an increased possibility of potential complications as the birth weight of the baby decreases.
- [W14.144] Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
- [W14.145] Monozygotic twins who share a placenta can develop twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.
- [W14.146] This condition means that blood from one twin is being diverted into the other twin.
- [W14.147] One twin, the 'donor' twin, is small and anemic, the other, the 'recipient' twin, is large and polycythemic.
- [W14.148] The lives of both twins are endangered by this condition.
- [W14.149] Stillbirths occurs when a fetus dies after 20 weeks of gestation.
- [W14.150] There are two types of stillbirth, including intrauterine death and intrapartum death.
- [W14.151] Intrauterine death occurs when a baby dies during late pregnancy.
- [W14.152] Intrapartum death, which is more common, occurs when a baby dies while the mother is giving birth.
- [W14.153] The cause of stillbirth is often unknown, but the rate of babies who are stillborn is higher in twins and multiple births.
- [W14.154] Caesareans or inductions are advised after 38 weeks of pregnancy for twins, because the risk of stillbirth increases after this time.
- [W14.155] Heterotopic pregnancy is an exceedingly rare type of dizygotic twinning in which one twin implants in the uterus as normal and the other remains in the fallopian tube as an ectopic pregnancy.
- [W14.156] Ectopic pregnancies must be resolved because they can be life-threatening to the mother.
- [W14.157] However, in most cases, the intrauterine pregnancy can be salvaged.
- [W14.158] For otherwise healthy twin pregnancies where both twins are head down, a trial of vaginal delivery is recommended at between 37 and 38 weeks.
- [W14.159] Vaginal delivery in this case does not worsen the outcome for the infant as compared with Caesarean section.
- [W14.160] There is controversy on the best method of delivery where the first twin is head first and the second is not.
- [W14.161] When the first twin is not head down a caesarean section is often recommended.
- [W14.162] It is estimated that 75% of twin pregnancies in the United States were delivered by caesarean section in 2008.
- [W14.163] In comparison, the rate of caesarean section for all pregnancies in the general population varies between 14% and 40%.
- [W14.164] In twins that share the same placenta, delivery may be considered at 36 weeks.
- [W14.165] For twins who are born early, there is insufficient evidence for or against placing preterm stable twins in the same cot or incubator (co-bedding).
- [W14.166] Twin studies are utilized in an attempt to determine how much of a particular trait is attributable to either genetics or environmental influence.
- [W14.167] These studies compare monozygotic and dizygotic twins for medical, genetic, or psychological characteristics to try to isolate genetic influence from epigenetic and environmental influence.
- [W14.168] Twins that have been separated early in life and raised in separate households are especially sought after for these studies, which have been used widely in the exploration of human nature.
- [W14.169] Classical twin studies are now being supplemented with molecular genetic studies which identify individual genes.
- [W14.170] This phenomenon is known as heteropaternal superfecundation.
- [W14.171] A 1992 study estimated from a sample of 127 cases that among dizygotic twins whose parents were involved in disputed parentage cases, the frequency of heteropaternal superfecundation was approximately 2.4%.
- [W14.172] Only one case has ever been recorded in Britain.
- [W14.173] Dizygotic twins from biracial couples can sometimes be mixed twins, which exhibit differing ethnic and racial features.
- [W14.174] One such pairing was born in London in 1993 to a white mother and Caribbean father.
- [W14.175] Monozygotic twins of different sexes
- [W14.176] Among monozygotic twins, in extremely rare cases, twins have been born with different sexes (one male, one female).
- [W14.177] When monozygotic twins are born with different sexes it is because of chromosomal defects.
- [W14.178] The probability of this is so small that multiples having different sexes is universally accepted as a sound basis for in utero clinical determination that the multiples are not monozygotic.
- [W14.179] Another abnormality that can result in monozygotic twins of different sexes is if the egg is fertilized by a male sperm but during cell division only the X chromosome is duplicated.
- [W14.180] This results in one normal male (XY) and one female with Turner syndrome (45,X).
- [W14.181] In these cases, although the twins did form from the same fertilized egg, it is incorrect to refer to them as genetically identical, since they have different karyotypes.
- [W14.182] Semi-identical (sesquizygotic) twins
- [W14.183] Monozygotic twins can develop differently, due to their genes being differently activated.
- [W14.184] More unusual are semi-identical twins, also known as sesquizygotic.
- [W14.185] As of 2019, only two cases have been reported.
- [W14.186] These "half-identical twins" are hypothesized to occur when an ovum is fertilized by two sperm (polyspermy).
- [W14.187] The cell assorts the chromosomes by heterogonesis and the cell divides into two, with each daughter cell now containing the correct number of chromosomes.
- [W14.188] The cells continue to develop into a morula.
- [W14.189] If the morula then undergoes a twinning event, two embryos will be formed, with different paternal genes but identical maternal genes.
- [W14.190] In 2007, a study reported a case of a pair of living twins, which shared an identical set of maternal chromosomes, while each having a distinct set of paternal chromosomes, albeit from the same man, and thus they most likely share half of their father's genetic makeup.
- [W14.191] The twins were both found to be chimeras.
- [W14.192] One was an intersex XX, and one an XY male.
- [W14.193] The exact mechanism of fertilization could not be determined but the study stated that it was unlikely to be a case of polar body twinning.
- [W14.194] The likely genetic basis of semi-identical twins was reported in 2019 by Michael Gabbett and Nicholas Fisk.
- [W14.195] In their seminal publication, Gabbett, Fisk and colleagues documented a second case of sesquizygosis and presented molecular evidence of the phenomenon.
- [W14.196] The reported twins shared 100% of their maternal chromosomes and 78% of their paternal genomic information.
- [W14.197] The authors presented evidence that two sperm from the same man fertilized an ovum simultaneously.
- [W14.198] The chromosomes assorted themselves through heterogonesis to form three cell lines.
- [W14.199] The purely paternal cell line died out due to genomic imprinting lethality, while the other two cell lines, each consisting of the same maternal DNA but only 50% identical paternal DNA, formed a morula which subsequently split into twins.
- [W14.200] Mirror image twins result when a fertilized egg splits later in the embryonic stage than normal timing, around day 9–12.
- [W14.201] This type of twinning could exhibit characteristics with reversed asymmetry, such as opposite dominant handedness, dental structure, or even organs (situs inversus).
- [W14.202] If the split occurs later than this time period, the twins risk being conjoined.
- [W14.203] There is no DNA-based zygosity test that can determine if twins are indeed mirror image.
- [W14.204] The term mirror image is used because the twins, when facing each other, appear as matching reflections.
- [W14.205] There have been many studies highlighting the development of language in twins compared to single-born children.
- [W14.206] These studies have converged on the notion that there is a greater rate of delay in language development in twins than in their single-born counterparts.
- [W14.207] The reasons for this are in question; however, cryptophasia was thought to be the major cause.
- [W14.208] Idioglossia is a private language that is usually invented by young children, specifically twins.
- [W14.209] Another term to describe what some people call twin talk is cryptophasia, in which a language is developed by twins that only they can understand.
- [W14.210] The increased focused communication between two twins may isolate them from their social environment.
- [W14.211] Idioglossia is rare and the attention of scientists has shifted away from this idea.
- [W14.212] However, some researchers and scientists say that cryptophasia or idioglossia is not rare.
- [W14.213] Researchers are looking into the impacts of a richer social environment for these twins to stimulate their development of language.
- [W14.214] Non-human dizygotic twinning is a common phenomenon in multiple animal species, including cats, dogs, cattle, bats, chimpanzees, and deer.
- [W14.215] This should not be confused with an animal's ability to produce a litter, because while litters are caused by the release of multiple eggs during an ovulation cycle, identical to the ovulation of dizygotic twins, they produce more than two offspring.
- [W14.216] Species such as sheep, goats, and deer have a higher propensity for dizygotic twinning, meaning that they carry a higher frequency of the allele responsible for the likelihood of twins, rather than the likelihood of litters (Whitcomb, 2021).
- [W14.217] Cases of monozygotic twinning in the animal kingdom are rare but have been recorded on a number of occasions.
- [W14.218] In 2016, a C-section of an Irish Wolfhound revealed identical twin puppies sharing a singular placenta.
- [W14.219] South African scientists, who were called in to study the identical twins wrote that...
- [W14.220] "To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of monozygotic twinning in the dog confirmed using DNA profiling." Additionally, armadillos have also been known to produce monozygotic twins, sometimes birthing two sets of identical twins during one reproductive cycle.
- [W14.221] Monozygotic twinning in armadillos functions as an evolutionary adaptation preventing inbreeding.
- [W14.222] Once an armadillo offspring enters its reproductive stage, the organism is forced to leave the nest in search of its mate, rather than mating with its siblings.
- [W14.223] Not only does monozygotic twinning dissuade from armadillo siblings inbreeding, but by forcing migration from the nest, this adaptation ensures the increased genetic variation and geographical population diffusion of armadillo species.
- [W14.224] Due to the increased parental investment provided for their offspring, larger mammals with longer life spans have slower reproductive cycles and tend to birth only one offspring at a time.
- [W14.225] This commonly repeated behavior in larger mammals evolved as a fixed, naturally-selected adaptation, resulting in a decreased twinning propensity in species such as giraffes, elephants, and hippopotami.
- [W14.226] Despite this adaptation, a case of rare monozygotic twinning has been documented in two elephant calves at the Bandipur Tiger Reserve in Karnataka, India.
- [W14.227] Chief Veterinarian of the Wildlife Trust of India, NVK Ashraf, in response to the twinning event, wrote that "in species that invest longer time in producing a baby, taking care of two twin calves will be difficult.
- [W14.228] Therefore, the incidence of twinning will be comparatively less."Ashraf's insight not only illuminates the rarity of twinning among large mammals in the natural world, but directs our attention to the increased twinning propensity of animals under human care.
- [W14.229] This increased twinning propensity is thought to be either caused by random mutation facilitated by genetic drift, or the positive selection of the "twinning" trait in human-controlled conditions.
- [W14.230] Due to the removal of natural predators and unpredictable environmental conditions with the increase of human-provided food and medical care, species residing in nature reserves, zoos, etc., carry an increased likelihood of reversing their naturally-selected traits that have been passed on for generations.
- [W14.231] When considering this phenomenon in relation to twinning, larger mammals not commonly associated with high twinning propensities can perhaps produce twins as an adaptive response to their human-controlled environment.
- [W14.232] Additionally, the high twinning propensity in species is thought to be positively correlated with the infant mortality rate of the reproducing organism's environment.
- [W14.233] Thus if a species lives in a controlled environment with a low infant mortality rate, the frequency of the "twinning trait" could increase, leading to a higher likelihood of producing twin offspring.
- [W14.234] In the case of the monozygotic twin calves in India, their existence could be connected to a new, positively selected adaptation of twinning attributed to species living under human care (Ward, 2014, p.
- [W14.235] Species with small physicalities and quick reproductive cycles carry high twinning propensities as a result of increased predation and high mortality rates.
- [W14.236] As scientists continue to study the origin of dizygotic twinning in the animal kingdom, many have turned to species that demonstrated an increased output of twins during periods of evolutionary distress and natural selection.
- [W14.237] Through their studies on Vespertilionidae and Cebidae species, scientists Guilherme Siniciato Terra Garbino and Marco Varella have proven that smaller species experiencing infertility in old age and/or unstable habits as a result of increased predation or human interference have undergone natural selection in gaining even higher twinning propensities.
- [W14.238] In his study on the evolution of litter size in bats, Garbino discovered that the vespertilionidae genus has higher twinning propensities as a result of their high roosting habitats.
- [W14.239] When tracked phylogenetically, scientists determined that the common ancestor of bats carried a higher twinning propensity which was then lost, and picked up again, eighteen times in evolutionary history.
- [W14.240] While other bat subfamilies such as Myotinae and Murinae inevitably lost the twinning trait, the family Vespertilionidae retained a high trait frequency due to mutation and environmental conditions that triggered natural selection.
- [W14.241] The height and exposed nature of Vespertilionidae's roosting locations resulted in a sharp increase in species mortality rate.
- [W14.242] Natural selection offsets these dangers by positively selecting high twinning propensity, resulting in not only Vespertilionidae's increased ability to produce twins but the increased likelihood of the genus's reproductive survival.
- [W14.243] This means that despite the family's high exposure to factors that would seemingly increase mortality rates, Vespertilionidae counteracts their environmental conditions through the evolutionary adaptation of dizygotic twins.
- [W14.244] The prevalence of dizygotic twinning in monkeys is thought to be an "insurance adaptation" for mothers reproducing at the end of their fertile years.
- [W14.245] While dizygotic twinning has been observed in species such as gorillas and chimpanzees, monkeys in the cebidae genus are found to be more likely to produce twins because of their small size and insect-based diet.
- [W14.246] This is because their small size indicates shorter gestation periods and the rapid maturation of offspring, resulting in a shorter lifespan where organisms are rapidly replaced by newer generations.
- [W14.247] The smaller size of the cebidae genus also makes these species more susceptible to predators, thus triggering the heightened pace of birth, maturation, reproduction, and death.
- [W14.248] Meanwhile, cebidae's insectivorous existence can be correlated with this genus's heightened ability to reproduce, as more resources become available, more organisms can take advantage of these resources.
- [W14.249] Thus, monkeys that are smaller and have more access to food, such as the cebidae genus, have the ability to produce more offspring at a quicker pace.
- [W14.250] In terms of dizygotic twinning, it has been observed that older mothers within the cebidae genus have a higher chance of producing twins than those at the beginning stages of their fertility.
- [W14.251] Despite their access to resources, the cebidae genus has a high mortality rate attributed to their size, meaning that in order to "keep up" their quickened lifecycle, they must produce an excess of offspring in ensuring generational survival.
- [W14.252] The positively-selected adaptation of twinning counteracts the genus's high mortality rate by giving older mothers the chance to produce more than one offspring.
- [W14.253] This not only increases the likelihood that one or more of these offspring will reach reproductive maturity, but gives the mother a chance to birth at least one viable offspring despite their age.
- [W14.254] Due to their short life cycles, the cebidae genus is more inclined to produce dizygotic twins in their older reproductive years, thus signaling that the trait of high twinning propensity is one that is passed down in service of this genus's survival.
- [W14.255] Twins in Society: Parents, Bodies, Space, and Talk (Palgrave Macmillan; 2010) 221 pages; explores the experience of child twins, adult twins, and parents of twins, with a focus on Britain.
