## [W24] Wikipedia: House mouse
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=House_mouse&oldid=1381076001 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W24.1] The house mouse (Mus musculus) is a small mammal of the rodent family Muridae, characteristically having a pointed snout, large rounded ears, and a long and almost hairless tail.
- [W24.2] It is one of the most abundant species of the genus Mus.
- [W24.3] Although a wild animal, the house mouse has benefited significantly from associating with human habitation to the point that truly wild populations are significantly less common than the synanthropic populations near human activity.
- [W24.4] The house mouse has been domesticated as the pet or fancy mouse, and as the laboratory mouse, which is one of the most important model organisms in biology and medicine.
- [W24.5] The complete mouse reference genome was sequenced in 2002.
- [W24.6] House mice have an adult body length (nose to base of tail) of 7.5–10 centimetres (3–4 in) and a tail length of 5–10 cm (2–4 in).
- [W24.7] The weight is typically 11–30 g (3⁄8–1 oz).
- [W24.8] In the wild they vary in color from grey and light brown to black (individual hairs are actually agouti coloured), but domesticated fancy mice and laboratory mice are produced in many colors ranging from white through champagne to pink.
- [W24.9] They have short hair and some, but not all, sub-species have a light belly.
- [W24.10] The ears and tail have little hair.
- [W24.11] The hind feet are short compared to Apodemus mice, only 15–19 mm (9⁄16–3⁄4 in) long; the normal gait is a run with a stride of about 4.5 cm (1+3⁄4 in), though they can jump vertically up to 45 cm (18 in).
- [W24.12] The voice is a high-pitched squeak.
- [W24.13] House mice thrive under a variety of conditions; they are found in and around homes and commercial structures, as well as in open fields and agricultural lands.
- [W24.14] Newborn males and females can be distinguished on close examination as the anogenital distance in males is about double that of the female.
- [W24.15] From the age of about ten days, females have five pairs of mammary glands and nipples; males have no nipples.
- [W24.16] When sexually mature, the most striking and obvious difference is the presence of testicles on the males.
- [W24.17] These are large compared to the rest of the body and can be retracted into the body.
- [W24.18] The tail, which is used for balance, has only a thin covering of hair as it is the main peripheral organ of heat loss in thermoregulation along with—to a lesser extent—the hairless parts of the paws and ears.
- [W24.19] Blood flow to the tail can be precisely controlled in response to changes in ambient temperature using a system of arteriovenous anastomoses to increase the temperature of the skin on the tail by as much as 10 °C (18 °F) to lose body heat.
- [W24.20] Tail length varies according to the environmental temperature of the mouse during postnatal development, so mice living in colder regions tend to have shorter tails.
- [W24.21] The tail is used for balance when the mouse is climbing or running, or as a base when the animal stands on its hind legs (tripoding), and to convey information about the dominance status of an individual in encounters with other mice.
- [W24.22] In addition to the regular pea-sized thymus organ in the chest, house mice have a second functional pinhead-sized thymus organ in the neck next to the trachea.
- [W24.23] Mice are boreoeutherian placental mammals of the Glires clade, which means they are amongst the closest relatives of humans other than lagomorphs, treeshrews, flying lemurs and other primates.
- [W24.24] The three widely accepted subspecies are increasingly treated as distinct species by some:
- [W24.25] Southeastern Asian house mouse (M. m. castaneus) (southern and southeastern Asia)
- [W24.26] Western European house mouse (M. m. domesticus); includes the fancy mouse and the laboratory mouse (Western Europe, North America, South America, Africa and Oceania)
- [W24.27] Eastern European house mouse (M. m. musculus) (Eastern Europe and northern Asia)
- [W24.28] Two additional subspecies have been recognized more recently:
- [W24.29] Southwestern Asian house mouse (M. m. bactrianus) (southwestern and Central Asia).
- [W24.30] However, due to significant genetic similarity observed between M. m. bactrianus and M. m. castaneus, the subspecies designation for M. m. bactrianus has now been questioned.
- [W24.31] Pygmy house mouse (M. m. gentilulus) (the Arabian Peninsula and Madagascar)
- [W24.32] Many more subspecies' names have been given to house mice, but these are now regarded as synonyms of the five subspecies.
- [W24.33] Some populations are hybrids of different subspecies, including the Japanese house mouse (M. m. molossinus).
- [W24.34] A notable region of hybridization is a region in general Europe where M. m. domesticus and M. m. musculus are often found to hybridize.
- [W24.35] However, male hybrid mice typically experience hybrid sterility, which maintains reproductive separation between the two subspecies.
- [W24.36] The standard species karyotype is composed of 40 chromosomes.
- [W24.37] Within Western Europe there are numerous populations – chromosomal races – with a reduced chromosome count arising from Robertsonian fusion.
- [W24.38] Suzuki et al., 2013 confirms the theory that M. musculus originates in Southwestern Asia and identifies 5 subspecies and their origins: musculus in northern Eurasia, castaneus in India and Southeast Asia, a previously unknown subspecies from Nepal, domesticus in western Europe, and gentilulus in Yemen.
- [W24.39] A recent study using 89 whole-genome sequences revealed that the modern day M. m. castaneus emerged from an ancestral M. musculus population in Indian subcontinent some time around 700 kya.
- [W24.40] From there, this ancestral population migrated to Iran around 360 kya to form M. m. domesticus and then to Afghanistan around 260 kya to form M. m. musculus.
- [W24.41] House mice usually run, walk, or stand on all fours, but when eating, fighting, or orienting themselves, they rear up on their hind legs with additional support from the tail – a behavior known as "tripoding".
- [W24.42] Mice are good jumpers, climbers, and swimmers, and are generally considered to be thigmotactic.
- [W24.43] Mice are mostly crepuscular or nocturnal and are averse to bright lights.
- [W24.44] The average sleep time of a captive house mouse is reported to be 12.5 hours per day.
- [W24.45] They live in a wide variety of hidden places near food sources, and construct nests from various soft materials.
- [W24.46] Mice are territorial, and one dominant male usually lives together with several females and young mice.
- [W24.47] Dominant males respect each other's territories, normally entering another's territory only if it is vacant.
- [W24.48] If two or more males are housed together in a cage, they often become aggressive unless they have been raised together from birth.
- [W24.49] House mice primarily feed on plant matter, but are omnivorous.
- [W24.50] They eat their own faeces to acquire nutrients produced by bacteria in their intestines.
- [W24.51] House mice, like most other rodents, can not vomit.
- [W24.52] Mice are generally afraid of rats, which often kill and eat them (muricide).
- [W24.53] Despite this, free-living populations of rats and mice do exist together in forest areas in New Zealand, North America, and elsewhere.
- [W24.54] House mice are generally poor competitors and in most areas cannot survive away from human settlements in areas where other small mammals, such as wood mice, are present.
- [W24.55] However, in some areas (such as Australia), mice are able to coexist with other small rodent species.
- [W24.56] The social behavior of the house mouse is not rigidly fixed into species-specific patterns but is instead adaptable to the environmental conditions, such as the availability of food and space.
- [W24.57] This adaptability allows house mice to inhabit diverse areas ranging from sandy dunes to apartment buildings.
- [W24.58] House mice have two forms of social behaviour, the expression of which depends on the environmental context.
- [W24.59] House mice in buildings and other urbanized areas with close proximity to humans are known as commensal.
- [W24.60] Commensal mice populations often have an excessive food source resulting in high population densities and small home ranges.
- [W24.61] This causes a switch from territorial behaviour to a hierarchy of individuals.
- [W24.62] When populations have an excess of food, there is less aggression between females, which usually occurs to gain access to food or to prevent infanticide.
- [W24.63] Aggression between males occurs in commensal populations, mainly to defend female mates and protect a small territory.
- [W24.64] The high level of male-to-male aggression, with a low female-to-female aggression level is common in polygamous populations.
- [W24.65] The social unit of commensal house mouse populations generally consists of one male and two or more females, usually related.
- [W24.66] These groups breed cooperatively, with the females communally nursing.
- [W24.67] This cooperative breeding and rearing by related females helps increase reproductive success.
- [W24.68] When there are no related females breeding groups can form from non-related females.
- [W24.69] In open areas such as shrubs and fields, the house mouse population is known as noncommensal.
- [W24.70] These populations are often limited by water or food supply and have large territories.
- [W24.71] Female-female aggression in the noncommensal house mouse populations is much higher, reaching a level generally attributed to free-ranging species.
- [W24.72] Male aggression is also higher in noncommensal populations.
- [W24.73] In commensal populations, males come into contact with other males quite frequently due to high population densities and aggression must be mediated or the risk of injury becomes too great.
- [W24.74] Both commensal and noncommensal house mouse males aggressively defend their territory and act to exclude all intruders.
- [W24.75] Males mark their territory by scent marking with urine.
- [W24.76] In marked territories, intruders showed significantly lower aggression than the territory residents.
- [W24.77] House mice show a male-biased dispersal; males generally leave their birth sites and migrate to form new territories whereas females generally stay and are opportunistic rather than seasonal breeders.
- [W24.78] The visual apparatus of mice is basically similar to that of humans but differs in that they are dichromats and have only two types of cone cells whereas humans are trichromats and have three.
- [W24.79] This means that mice do not perceive some of the colors in the human visual spectrum.
- [W24.80] However, the ventral area of the mouse retina has a much greater density of ultraviolet-sensitive cones than other areas of the retina, although the biological significance of this structure is unknown.
- [W24.81] In 2007, mice genetically engineered to produce the third type of cone were shown to be able to distinguish a range of colors similar to that perceived by tetrachromats.
- [W24.82] House mice also rely on pheromones for social communication, some of which are produced by the preputial glands of both sexes.
- [W24.83] The tear fluid and urine of male mice also contains pheromones, such as major urinary proteins.
- [W24.84] Mice detect pheromones mainly with the vomeronasal organ (Jacobson's organ), located at the bottom of the nose.
- [W24.85] The urine of house mice, especially that of males, has a characteristic strong odor.
- [W24.86] At least 10 different compounds, such as alkanes, alcohols, etc., are detectable in the urine.
- [W24.87] Among them, five compounds are specific to males, namely 3-cyclohexene-1-methanol, aminotriazole (3-amino-s-triazole), 4-ethyl phenol, 3-ethyl-2,7-dimethyl octane and 1-iodoundecane.
- [W24.88] Odours from adult males or from pregnant or lactating females can speed up or retard sexual maturation in juvenile females and synchronise reproductive cycles in mature females (i.e. the Whitten effect).
- [W24.89] Odours of unfamiliar male mice may terminate pregnancies, i.e. the Bruce effect.
- [W24.90] Mice can sense surfaces and air movements with their whiskers which are also used during thigmotaxis.
- [W24.91] If mice are blind from birth, super-normal growth of the vibrissae occurs presumably as a compensatory response.
- [W24.92] Conversely, if the vibrissae are absent, the use of vision is intensified.
- [W24.93] Life cycle and reproduction
- [W24.94] Female house mice have an estrous cycle about four to six days long, with estrus itself lasting less than a day.
- [W24.95] If several females are held together under crowded conditions, they will often not have an estrus at all.
- [W24.96] If they are then exposed to male urine, they will come into estrus after 72 hours.
- [W24.97] Male house mice court females by emitting characteristic ultrasonic calls in the 30 kHz–110 kHz range.
- [W24.98] The calls are most frequent during courtship when the male is sniffing and following the female; however, the calls continue after mating has begun, at which time the calls are coincident with mounting behaviour.
- [W24.99] Males can be induced to emit these calls by female pheromones.
- [W24.100] The vocalizations appear to differ between individuals and have been compared to bird songs because of their complexity.
- [W24.101] While females have the capability to produce ultrasonic calls, they typically do not do so during mating behaviour.
- [W24.102] Following copulation, female mice will normally develop a mating plug which prevents further copulation.
- [W24.103] The plug is not necessary for pregnancy initiation, as this will also occur without the plug.
- [W24.104] The presence or absence of the plug will not affect litter size either.
- [W24.105] This plug stays in place for some 24 hours.
- [W24.106] The gestation period is about 19–21 days, and they give birth to a litter of 3–14 young (average six to eight).
- [W24.107] One female can have 5 to 10 litters per year, so the mouse population can increase very quickly.
- [W24.108] Breeding occurs throughout the year.
- [W24.109] (However, animals living in the wild do not reproduce in the colder months, even though they do not hibernate.)
- [W24.110] The pups are born blind and without fur or ears.
- [W24.111] The ears are fully developed by the fourth day, fur begins to appear at about six days and the eyes open around 13 days after birth; the pups are weaned at around 21 days.
- [W24.112] Females reach sexual maturity at about six weeks of age and males at about eight weeks, but both can copulate as early as five weeks.
- [W24.113] Although house mice can be either monogamous or polygamous, they are most commonly polygamous.
- [W24.114] They generally show characteristics of mate-defense polygyny in that males are highly territorial and protective of their mates, while females are less agonistic.
- [W24.115] The communal nursing groups that result from these behaviors lead to lower numbers of infanticide since more females are able to protect greater numbers of offspring.
- [W24.116] Evolutionary and behavioural consequences
- [W24.117] Both evolutionary and behavioral consequences result from the polygamous nature of the house mouse.
- [W24.118] One consequence is the paternal investment, which is lower in polygamous mice than in mice that are monogamous.
- [W24.119] This occurs due to the fact that males spend more time involved in sexual competition than do females, leaving less time for paternal care.
- [W24.120] Polygamous male house mice spend less time alone with pups.
- [W24.121] They are also less likely and slower to retrieve lost pups than males of monogamous mice.
- [W24.122] In contrast, the maternal investment is similar between female mice that have mated once versus multiply.
- [W24.123] The polygamous behavior of female house mice promotes sperm competition, which affects both male and female evolutionary fitness.
- [W24.124] Females who mate with multiple males tend to produce both pups in greater numbers, and with higher survival rates, increasing female fitness.
- [W24.125] Sperm competition that arises from polygamy favors males with faster, more motile sperm in higher numbers, increasing male fitness.
- [W24.126] The competitive aspect of insemination increases the frequency of polyandrous events and fertilizations.
- [W24.127] Polyandry has evolved to increase reproductive success.
- [W24.128] Male mating behavior is also affected in response to the practice of polygamous behavior.
- [W24.129] Compared to monogamous house mice, polygamous house mice mate for longer periods of time.
- [W24.130] This behaviour allows for an increase in both the transfer of sperm and paternity success, which in turn increases male fitness.
- [W24.131] As opposed to polygyny, polyandrous behavior in females is the act of breeding with several males in the same season.
- [W24.132] Variation in number of males that females mate with occurs among a population.
- [W24.133] Polyandrous behavior is a common mating pattern in the subspecies M. m. musculus as well as its relative M. m. domesticus.
- [W24.134] Polyandry occurs in 30% of all wild populations of house mice.
- [W24.135] Litters from multiple sires tend to be more genetically diverse than litters of single sires.
- [W24.136] Multiple paternity is also more common in larger populations than smaller populations, because there is a larger number of mates and more diverse mates to choose from.
- [W24.137] Within a population, males and females show different levels of multiple mating.
- [W24.138] Females show bias toward unrelated males rather than related males during sexual selection, resulting in more genetically diverse offspring and a reduction of inbreeding depression.
- [W24.139] Inbreeding depression increases genetic incompatibilities, levels of homozygosity, and the chance of expression of deleterious recessive alleles.
- [W24.140] Polyandry has been shown to increase offspring survival compared to monandry.
- [W24.141] The fitness of females increases in polyandrous lines due to more genetic diversity and greater litter size.
- [W24.142] Due to polyandry, males can be confused by the identity of new offspring.
- [W24.143] Multiple mating by females and paternity confusion can decrease rates of infanticide.
- [W24.144] If the males are uncertain if the offspring are theirs, they are less likely to kill the offspring.
- [W24.145] Intrauterine insemination causes an evolutionary consequence resulting from polyandrous behavior.
- [W24.146] When multiple males mate with one female, there are multiple sets of sperm gametes in a female mouse.
- [W24.147] Offspring fertilized by multiple males can compete more strongly for mother's resources and can lead to a decrease in body size and variation in body size.
- [W24.148] Since inbreeding is detrimental, it tends to be avoided.
- [W24.149] In the house mouse, the major urinary protein (MUP) gene cluster provides a highly polymorphic scent signal of genetic identity that appears to underlie kin recognition and inbreeding avoidance.
- [W24.150] Thus there are fewer matings between mice sharing MUP haplotypes than would be expected if there were random mating.
- [W24.151] Another mechanism for avoiding inbreeding is evident when a female house mouse mates with multiple males.
- [W24.152] In such a case, there appears to be egg-driven sperm selection against sperm from related males.
- [W24.153] As a model organism, a great deal is known about mouse genetics, with a major tool being the knockout mouse technique.
- [W24.154] House mice usually live less than one year in the wild, due to a high level of predation and exposure to harsh environments.
- [W24.155] In protected environments, however, they often live two to three years.
- [W24.156] The Methuselah Mouse Prize is a competition to breed or engineer extremely long-lived laboratory mice.
- [W24.157] As of 2005, the record holder was a genetically engineered mouse that lived for 1,819 days (7 days short of 5 years).
- [W24.158] Another record holder that was kept in an enriched environment but did not receive any genetic, pharmacological, or dietary treatment lived for 1,551 days (4 years, 90 days).
- [W24.159] In several different mouse strains, with age, nuclear DNA from the liver, heart, brain, kidney, skeletal muscle and spleen showed significantly higher levels of 8-Oxo-2'-deoxyguanosine (8-oxo-dG), a direct marker of DNA damage.
- [W24.160] This increase was attributed to an increase in sensitivity of these tissues to oxidative stress.
- [W24.161] Caloric restriction is known to increase the lifespan of rodents and to reduce aging.
- [W24.162] A study conducted with mice undergoing dietary restriction was found to significantly reduce the age-related accumulation of 8-oxo-dG levels in all tissues studied when compared with a control.
- [W24.163] Thus, it has been suggested that oxidative DNA damage as a result of normal cellular metabolism could be a highly relevant factor of aging.
- [W24.164] In another study, two forms of DNA damage (8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine and DNA-protein crosslinks) were also found to increase with age in mouse brain and liver tissues.
- [W24.165] House mice usually live in proximity to humans, in or around houses and/or fields.
- [W24.166] They are native to India, and later they spread to the eastern Mediterranean about 13,000 BC, only spreading into the rest of Europe around 1000 BC.
- [W24.167] This time lag is thought to be because the mice require agrarian human settlements above a certain size.
- [W24.168] The house mouse first arrived in the Americas in the early sixteenth century.
- [W24.169] It was carried aboard on the ships of Spanish explorers and Conquistadors.
- [W24.170] About one hundred years later, it arrived in North America with French fur traders and English colonists.
- [W24.171] They have since been spread to all parts of the globe by humans.
- [W24.172] Many studies have been done on mouse phylogenies to reconstruct early human movements.
- [W24.173] For example, one study suggests the possibility of a previously unsuspected early link between Northern Europe and Madeira on the basis of the origin of Madeiran mice.
- [W24.174] House mice were thought to be the primary reason for the domestication of cats.
- [W24.175] The first written reference to mice kept as pets occurs in the Erya, the oldest extant Chinese dictionary, from a mention in an 1100 BC version.
- [W24.176] Human domestication led to numerous strains of "fancy" or hobby mice with a variety of colours and a docile temperament.
- [W24.177] Domestic varieties of the house mouse are bred as a food source for some carnivorous pet reptiles, birds, arthropods, and fish.
- [W24.178] The effects of domestication can be rapid, with captive-reared mice differing in boldness and activity patterns compared to wild-caught mice after 4–5 generations in recent research.
- [W24.179] Mice are widespread pest organisms, and one of the most common rodents to infest human buildings.
- [W24.180] They commonly forage outdoors during the spring and summer, but retreat into buildings through the autumn and winter to seek warmth and food.
- [W24.181] They typically feed on unattended food, leftovers and garden produce.
- [W24.182] Their foraging risks the contamination and degradation of food supplies, and can also spread other pests such as fleas, ticks, lice and mites.
- [W24.183] When infesting homes, house mice may pose a risk of damaging and compromising the structure of furniture and the building itself.
- [W24.184] They gnaw various materials to file down their growing teeth and keep the length under control.
- [W24.185] Common damage includes gnawed electrical wires, marks on wooden furniture and construction supporting elements, and textile damage.
- [W24.186] House mice can transmit diseases, contaminate food, and damage food packaging.
- [W24.187] The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention provides a list of diseases transmitted by all rodents, a few of which are transmitted through the house mouse.
- [W24.188] Lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCMV) can be transmitted by mice, but is not commonly reported in humans.
- [W24.189] Most human infections are mild and are often never diagnosed.
- [W24.190] There are concerns that women infected with LCMV during pregnancy are at risk.
- [W24.191] House mice are not usually a vector of bubonic plague (Black Death) because they have fewer infestations with fleas than do rats, and because the fleas which house mice normally carry exhibit little tendency to bite humans rather than their natural host.
- [W24.192] Rickettsialpox, caused by the bacterium Rickettsia akari and similar to chickenpox, is spread by mice in general, but is very rare and generally mild and resolves within two or three weeks if untreated.
- [W24.193] No known deaths have resulted from the disease.
- [W24.194] Murine typhus (also called endemic typhus), caused by the bacterium Rickettsia typhi, is transmitted by the fleas that infest rats.
- [W24.195] While rat fleas are the most common vectors, cat fleas and mouse fleas are less common modes of transmission.
- [W24.196] Endemic typhus is highly treatable with antibiotics.
- [W24.197] CDC currently does not mention rickettsialpox or murine typhus on its website about diseases directly transmitted by rodents in general.
- [W24.198] Leptospirosis is carried by a variety of wild and domestic animals including dogs, rats, swine, cattle, mice in general, and can be transmitted by the urine of an infected animal and is contagious as long as the urine is still moist.
- [W24.199] In Central Europe, the Dobrava sequence of hantavirus has been found in house mice.
- [W24.200] Mice play a role in the ecological cycle of Lyme disease by acting as hosts for tick larvae, thereby contributing indirectly to transmission.
- [W24.201] When young ticks feed on infected mice, they acquire the bacteria responsible for the disease; as the ticks mature, they can transmit the infection to humans and other animals through bites.
- [W24.202] Mice have become an invasive species on islands to where they have spread during the period of European exploration and colonisation.
- [W24.203] New Zealand had no land mammals other than two species of bat, though several marsupials, prior to human occupation, and the house mouse is one of many mammalian species that have been introduced.
- [W24.204] Mice are responsible for a reduction in native bird species since they eat some of the same foods as birds.
- [W24.205] They are also known to kill lizards and have a large effect on native insects.
- [W24.206] Gough Island in the South Atlantic is used by 20 species of seabirds for breeding, including almost all of the world's Tristan albatross (Diomedea dabbenena) and Atlantic petrel (Pterodroma incerta).
- [W24.207] Until house mice arrived on the island in the 19th century with sailors, the birds did not have any mammalian predators.
- [W24.208] The mice have since grown unusually large and have learned to attack albatross chicks, which can be 90 cm tall, but are largely immobile, by working in groups and gnawing on them until they bleed to death.
- [W24.209] In the grain belt of southeastern Australia, the introduced subspecies M. m. domesticus breed so successfully, every three years or so they reach plague proportions, achieving densities of 1000 per hectare and causing massive disruption to communities, and losses to agriculture of A$36 million annually.
- [W24.210] Mice are the most commonly used mammalian laboratory animal, due to their relatively close relationship, and associated high homology, with humans, their ease in maintenance and handling, and their high rate of reproduction.
- [W24.211] Laboratory mice typically belong to standardized inbred strains selected for the stability or clarity of specific harmful mutations.
- [W24.212] This allows research with laboratory mice to easily restrict genetic and biological variables, making them very useful model organisms in genetic and medicinal research.
- [W24.213] Mice have been used in scientific research since the 1650s.
- [W24.214] Importance of mice as a house and agricultural pest resulted in a development of a variety of mouse-related rituals and stories in world's cultures.
- [W24.215] The Ancient Egyptians had a story about "The mouse as vizier".
- [W24.216] Many South Slavs had a traditional annual "Mouse Day" celebration.
- [W24.217] In the eastern Balkans (most of Bulgaria, North Macedonia, the Torlak districts of Serbia), the "Mouse Day" (Bulgarian: Миши ден, Мишин ден) was celebrated on 9 October of the Julian calendar (corresponds to 27 October of the Gregorian calendar in the 20th and 21st centuries), the next day after the feast of Saint Demetrius.
- [W24.218] In the western Balkans (Bosnia, Croatia), the Mouse Day would usually be celebrated in the spring, during the Maslenitsa week or early in the Lent.
- [W24.219] Myobia musculi, common mite found in fur of house mouse
- [W24.220] "Auditory Communication among Adults".
- [W24.221] Handbook of Mouse Auditory Research: From Behavior to Molecular Biology.
- [W24.222] Ensembl Mus musculus genome browser, from the Ensembl Project

## [W25] Wikipedia: Duck
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Duck&oldid=1382173698 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W25.1] Duck is the common name for numerous species of waterfowl in the family Anatidae.
- [W25.2] Ducks are generally smaller and shorter-necked than swans and geese, which are members of the same family.
- [W25.3] Divided among several subfamilies, they are a form taxon; they do not represent a monophyletic group (the group of all descendants of a single common ancestral species), since swans and geese are not considered ducks.
- [W25.4] Ducks are mostly aquatic birds and may be found in both fresh water and sea water.
- [W25.5] Ducks are sometimes confused with several types of unrelated water birds with similar forms, such as loons or divers, grebes, gallinules and coots.
- [W25.6] The word duck comes from Old English dūce 'diver', a derivative of the verb *dūcan 'to duck, bend down low as if to get under something, or dive', because of the way many species in the dabbling duck group feed by upending; compare with Dutch duiken and German tauchen 'to dive'.
- [W25.7] This word replaced Old English ened /ænid 'duck', possibly to avoid confusion with other words, such as ende 'end' with similar forms.
- [W25.8] Other Germanic languages still have similar words for duck, for example, Dutch eend, German Ente and Norwegian and.
- [W25.9] The word ened /ænid was inherited from Proto-Indo-European; cf. Latin anas (stem anat-) "duck", Lithuanian ántis 'duck', Ancient Greek νῆσσα /νῆττα (nēssa /nētta) 'duck', and Sanskrit ātí 'water bird', among others.
- [W25.10] A duckling is a young duck in downy plumage or baby duck, but in the food trade a young domestic duck which has just reached adult size and bulk and its meat is still fully tender, is sometimes labelled as a duckling.
- [W25.11] A male is called a drake and the female is called a duck, or in ornithology a hen.
- [W25.12] All ducks belong to the biological order Anseriformes, a group that contains the ducks, geese and swans, as well as the screamers, and the magpie goose.
- [W25.13] All except the screamers belong to the biological family Anatidae.
- [W25.14] Within the family, ducks are split into a variety of subfamilies and "tribes".
- [W25.15] The number and composition of these subfamilies and tribes is the cause of considerable disagreement among taxonomists.
- [W25.16] Some base their decisions on morphological characteristics, others on shared behaviours or genetic studies.
- [W25.17] The number of suggested subfamilies containing ducks ranges from two to five.
- [W25.18] The significant level of hybridisation that occurs among wild ducks complicates efforts to tease apart the relationships between various species.
- [W25.19] In most modern classifications, the so-called "true ducks" belong to the subfamily Anatinae, which is further split into a varying number of tribes.
- [W25.20] The largest of these, the Anatini, contains the "dabbling" or "river" ducks –  named for their method of feeding primarily at the surface of fresh water.
- [W25.21] The "diving ducks", also named for their primary feeding method, make up the tribe Aythyini.
- [W25.22] The "sea ducks" of the tribe Mergini are diving ducks which specialise on fish and shellfish and spend a majority of their lives in saltwater.
- [W25.23] The tribe Oxyurini contains the "stifftails", diving ducks notable for their small size and stiff, upright tails.
- [W25.24] A number of other species called ducks are not considered to be "true ducks" and are typically placed in other subfamilies or tribes.
- [W25.25] The whistling ducks are assigned either to a tribe (Dendrocygnini) in the subfamily Anatinae or the subfamily Anserinae, or to their own subfamily (Dendrocygninae) or family (Dendrocyganidae).
- [W25.26] The freckled duck of Australia is either the sole member of the tribe Stictonettini in the subfamily Anserinae, or in its own family, the Stictonettinae.
- [W25.27] The shelducks make up the tribe Tadornini in the family Anserinae in some classifications, and their own subfamily, Tadorninae, in others, while the steamer ducks are either placed in the family Anserinae in the tribe Tachyerini or lumped with the shelducks in the tribe Tadorini.
- [W25.28] The perching ducks make up in the tribe Cairinini in the subfamily Anserinae in some classifications, while that tribe is eliminated in other classifications and its members assigned to the tribe Anatini.
- [W25.29] The torrent duck is generally included in the subfamily Anserinae in the monotypic tribe Merganettini, but is sometimes included in the tribe Tadornini.
- [W25.30] The pink-eared duck is sometimes included as a true duck either in the tribe Anatini or the tribe Malacorhynchini, and other times is included with the shelducks in the tribe Tadornini.
- [W25.31] The overall body plan of ducks is elongated and broad, and they are also relatively long-necked, albeit not as long-necked as the geese and swans.
- [W25.32] The body shape of diving ducks varies somewhat from this in being more rounded.
- [W25.33] The bill is usually broad and contains serrated pectens, which are particularly well defined in the filter-feeding species.
- [W25.34] In the case of some fishing species the bill is long and strongly serrated.
- [W25.35] The scaled legs are strong and well developed, and generally set far back on the body, more so in the highly aquatic species, which typically feature webbed feet.
- [W25.36] The wings are very strong and are generally short and pointed, and the flight of ducks requires fast continuous strokes, requiring in turn strong wing muscles.
- [W25.37] Three species of steamer duck are almost flightless, however.
- [W25.38] Many species of duck are temporarily flightless while moulting; they seek out protected habitat with good food supplies during this period.
- [W25.39] This moult typically precedes migration.
- [W25.40] The drakes of northern species often have extravagant plumage, but that is moulted in summer to give a more female-like appearance, the "eclipse" plumage.
- [W25.41] Southern resident species typically show less sexual dimorphism, although there are exceptions such as the paradise shelduck of New Zealand, which is both strikingly sexually dimorphic and in which the female's plumage is brighter than that of the male.
- [W25.42] The plumage of juvenile birds generally resembles that of the female.
- [W25.43] Female ducks have evolved to have a corkscrew shaped vagina to prevent forced copulations.
- [W25.44] Ducks have a cosmopolitan distribution, and are found on every continent except Antarctica.
- [W25.45] Several species manage to live on subantarctic islands, including South Georgia and the Auckland Islands.
- [W25.46] Ducks have reached a number of isolated oceanic islands, including the Hawaiian Islands, Micronesia and the Galápagos Islands, where they are often vagrants and less often residents.
- [W25.47] A handful are endemic to such far-flung islands.
- [W25.48] Some duck species, mainly those breeding in the temperate and Arctic Northern Hemisphere, are migratory; those in the tropics are generally not.
- [W25.49] Some ducks, particularly in Australia where rainfall is erratic, are nomadic, seeking out the temporary lakes and pools that form after localised heavy rain.
- [W25.50] Ducks eat food sources such as grasses, aquatic plants, fish, insects, small amphibians, worms, and small molluscs.
- [W25.51] Dabbling ducks feed on the surface of water or on land, or as deep as they can reach by up-ending without completely submerging.
- [W25.52] Along the edge of the bill, there is a comb-like structure called a pecten.
- [W25.53] This strains the water squirting from the side of the bill and traps any food.
- [W25.54] The pecten is also used to preen feathers and to hold slippery food items.
- [W25.55] Diving ducks and sea ducks forage deep underwater.
- [W25.56] To be able to submerge more easily, the diving ducks are heavier than dabbling ducks, and therefore have more difficulty taking off to fly.
- [W25.57] A few specialized species such as the mergansers are adapted to catch and swallow large fish.
- [W25.58] The others have the characteristic wide flat bill adapted to dredging-type jobs such as pulling up waterweed, pulling worms and small molluscs out of mud, searching for insect larvae, and bulk jobs such as dredging out, holding, turning head first, and swallowing a squirming frog.
- [W25.59] To avoid injury when digging into sediment it has no cere, but the nostrils come out through hard horn.
- [W25.60] The Guardian published an article advising that ducks should not be fed with bread because it damages the health of the ducks and pollutes waterways.
- [W25.61] Sandra C. Mitchell, DVM, DABVP suggests, with water: small fish, snails, crabs, insects, slugs, chopped lettuce, chopped cabbage, cracked corn, sliced grapes, frozen peas, cooked oats, cooked rice, grass seed, or commercial duck feed.
- [W25.62] Ducks generally only have one partner at a time, although the partnership usually only lasts one year.
- [W25.63] Larger species and the more sedentary species (like fast-river specialists) tend to have pair-bonds that last numerous years.
- [W25.64] Most duck species breed once a year, choosing to do so in favourable conditions (spring/summer or wet seasons).
- [W25.65] Ducks also tend to make a nest before breeding, and, after hatching, lead their ducklings to water.
- [W25.66] Mother ducks are very caring and protective of their young, but may abandon some of their ducklings if they are physically stuck in an area they cannot get out of (such as nesting in an enclosed courtyard) or are not prospering due to genetic defects or sickness brought about by hypothermia, starvation, or disease.
- [W25.67] Ducklings can also be orphaned by inconsistent late hatching where a few eggs hatch after the mother has abandoned the nest and led her ducklings to water.
- [W25.68] Female mallard ducks (as well as several other species in the genus Anas, such as the American and Pacific black ducks, spot-billed duck, northern pintail and common teal) make the classic "quack" sound while males make a similar but raspier sound that is sometimes written as "breeeeze", but, despite widespread misconceptions, most species of duck do not "quack".
- [W25.69] In general, ducks make a range of calls, including whistles, cooing, yodels and grunts.
- [W25.70] For example, the scaup – which are diving ducks – make a noise like "scaup" (hence their name).
- [W25.71] Calls may be loud displaying calls or quieter contact calls.
- [W25.72] A common urban legend claims that duck quacks do not echo; however, this has been proven to be false.
- [W25.73] This myth was first debunked by the Acoustics Research Centre at the University of Salford in 2003 as part of the British Association's Festival of Science.
- [W25.74] It was also debunked in one of the earlier episodes of the popular Discovery Channel television show MythBusters.
- [W25.75] Ducks have many predators.
- [W25.76] Ducklings are particularly vulnerable, since their inability to fly makes them easy prey not only for predatory birds but also for large fish like pike, crocodilians, predatory testudines such as the alligator snapping turtle, and other aquatic hunters, including fish-eating birds such as herons.
- [W25.77] Ducks' nests are raided by land-based predators, and brooding females may be caught unaware on the nest by mammals, such as foxes, or large birds, such as hawks or owls.
- [W25.78] Adult ducks are fast fliers, but may be caught on the water by large aquatic predators including big fish such as the North American muskie and the European pike.
- [W25.79] In flight, ducks are safe from all but a few predators such as humans and the peregrine falcon, which uses its speed and strength to catch ducks.
- [W25.80] Humans have hunted ducks since prehistoric times.
- [W25.81] Excavations of middens in California dating to 7800–6400 BP have turned up bones of ducks, including at least one now-extinct flightless species.
- [W25.82] Ducks were captured in "significant numbers" by Holocene inhabitants of the lower Ohio River valley, suggesting they took advantage of the seasonal bounty provided by migrating waterfowl.
- [W25.83] Neolithic hunters in locations as far apart as the Caribbean, Scandinavia, Egypt, Switzerland and China relied on ducks as a source of protein for some or all of the year.
- [W25.84] Archeological evidence shows that Māori people in New Zealand hunted the flightless Finsch's duck, possibly to extinction, though rat predation may also have contributed to its fate.
- [W25.85] A similar end awaited the Chatham duck, a species with reduced flying capabilities which went extinct shortly after its island was colonised by Polynesian settlers.
- [W25.86] It is probable that duck eggs were gathered by Neolithic hunter-gathers as well, though hard evidence of this is uncommon.
- [W25.87] In many areas, wild ducks (including ducks farmed and released into the wild) are hunted for food or sport, by shooting, or by being trapped using duck decoys.
- [W25.88] Because an idle floating duck or a duck squatting on land cannot react to fly or move quickly, "a sitting duck" has come to mean "an easy target".
- [W25.89] These ducks may be contaminated by pollutants such as PCBs.
- [W25.90] Ducks have many economic uses, being farmed for their meat, eggs, and feathers (particularly their down).
- [W25.91] Approximately 3 billion ducks are slaughtered each year for meat worldwide.
- [W25.92] They are also kept and bred by aviculturists and often displayed in zoos.
- [W25.93] Almost all the varieties of domestic ducks are descended from the mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), apart from the Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata).
- [W25.94] The Call duck is another example of a domestic duck breed.
- [W25.95] Its name comes from its original use established by hunters, as a decoy to attract wild mallards from the sky, into traps set for them on the ground.
- [W25.96] The call duck is the world's smallest domestic duck breed, as it weighs less than 1 kg (2.2 lb).
- [W25.97] Ducks appear on several coats of arms, including the coat of arms of Lubāna (Latvia) and the coat of arms of Föglö (Åland).
- [W25.98] In 2002, psychologist Richard Wiseman and colleagues at the University of Hertfordshire, UK, finished a year-long LaughLab experiment, concluding that of all animals, ducks attract the most humor and silliness; he said: "If you're going to tell a joke involving an animal, make it a duck." The word "duck" may have become an inherently funny word in many languages, possibly because ducks are seen as silly in their looks or behavior.
- [W25.99] Of the many ducks in fiction, many are cartoon characters, such as Walt Disney's Donald Duck, and Warner Bros.' Daffy Duck.
- [W25.100] Howard the Duck started as a comic book character in 1973 and was made into a movie in 1986.
- [W25.101] The 1992 Disney film The Mighty Ducks, starring Emilio Estevez, chose the duck as the mascot for the fictional youth hockey team who are protagonists of the movie, based on the duck being described as a fierce fighter.
- [W25.102] This led to the duck becoming the nickname and mascot for the eventual National Hockey League professional team of the Anaheim Ducks, who were founded with the name the Mighty Ducks of Anaheim.
- [W25.103] The duck is also the nickname of the University of Oregon sports teams as well as the Long Island Ducks minor league baseball team.
- [W25.104] list of books (useful looking abstracts)
- [W25.105] Ducks on postage stamps Archived 2013-05-13 at the Wayback Machine
- [W25.106] Ducks at a Distance, by Rob Hines at Project Gutenberg - A modern illustrated guide to identification of US waterfowl

## [W26] Wikipedia: Mandarin duck
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mandarin_duck&oldid=1380677894 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W26.1] The mandarin duck (Aix galericulata) is a perching duck species native to East and Northeast Asia.
- [W26.2] It is sexually dimorphic; the males are elaborately coloured, while the females have more subdued colours.
- [W26.3] It is a medium-sized duck, at 41–49 cm (16–19 in) long with a 65–75 cm (26–30 in) wingspan.
- [W26.4] It is closely related to the North American wood duck, the only other member of the genus Aix. 'Aix' is an Ancient Greek word which was used by Aristotle to refer to an unknown diving bird, and 'galericulata' is the Latin for a wig, derived from galerum, a cap or bonnet.
- [W26.5] Outside of its native range, the mandarin duck has a large introduced population in the British Isles and Western Europe, with additional smaller introductions in North America.
- [W26.6] The mandarin duck was described and illustrated in 1727 by the German explorer Engelbert Kaempfer in his The History of Japan.
- [W26.7] He wrote: "Of Ducks also there are several differing kinds, and as tame as the Geese.
- [W26.8] One kind particularly I cannot forbear mentioning, because of the surprising beauty of its male, call'd Kinmodsui, which is so great, that being shew'd its picture in colours, I could hardly believe my own Eyes, till I saw the Bird it self, it being a very common one." In 1747 the English naturalist George Edwards included an illustration and a description of the species in the second volume of his A Natural History of Uncommon Birds.
- [W26.9] He used the English name "The Chinese teal".
- [W26.10] He based his hand-coloured etching on a live specimen kept by the merchant Matthew Decker on his estate at Richmond in Surrey.
- [W26.11] Decker was a director of the East India Company.
- [W26.12] When in 1758 the Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus updated his Systema Naturae for the tenth edition, he placed the mandarin duck with the ducks and geese in the genus Anas.
- [W26.13] Linnaeus included a brief description, coined the binomial name Anas galericulata and cited the earlier publications.
- [W26.14] The mandarin duck is now placed together with the wood duck in the genus Aix that was introduced in 1828 by the German ornithologist Friedrich Boie.
- [W26.15] The species is monotypic: no subspecies are recognised.
- [W26.16] The genus name is the Ancient Greek word for an unknown diving bird mentioned by Aristotle.
- [W26.17] The specific epithet is from Latin galericulatum meaning a "peruke" or "wig".
- [W26.18] Mandarin duck unusually has 84 chromosomes, all acrocentric, compared to 80, often submetacentric, for other ducks; this makes successful hybridisation with other ducks very difficult, and possibly impossible, though this is disputed.
- [W26.19] Hybrids have been reported with six other duck species, but none of these have yet been verified.
- [W26.20] The mandarin duck is among the smaller species of waterfowl, with a shorter body and smaller overall body size than most dabbling ducks, and is slightly smaller than its American wood duck relative.
- [W26.21] The adult male has a small red bill, large white crescent above the eye and reddish face and "whiskers".
- [W26.22] The male's breast is purple with two vertical white bars, the flanks ruddy, and has two orange 'sail' feathers at the back (modified 12th secondary flight feathers whose enlarged medial vane sticks up similar to boat sails).
- [W26.23] The female is similar to the female wood duck, with greyish-brown plumage, and a slender white eye-ring and stripe running back from the eye.
- [W26.24] The female is paler on the underside, has a small white flank stripe, and a pale tip to its bill.
- [W26.25] Both the males and females have crests, but the purple crest is more pronounced on the male.
- [W26.26] Like many other species of ducks, the male undergoes a moult after the mating season into eclipse plumage.
- [W26.27] When in eclipse plumage, the male looks similar to the female, but can be distinguished by its bright yellow-orange or red beak, lack of any crest, and a less pronounced eye-stripe.
- [W26.28] Mandarin duck ducklings are almost identical in appearance to wood duck ducklings, and very similar to mallard ducklings.
- [W26.29] The ducklings can be distinguished from mallard ducklings because the eye-stripe of mandarin duck ducklings (and wood duck ducklings) stops at the eye, while in mallard ducklings it reaches all the way to the bill.
- [W26.30] The species was once widespread in East Asia, but large-scale exports and the destruction of its forest habitat had reduced populations in eastern Russia and in China to below 1,000 pairs in each country by the 1980s; Japan, however, was thought to still hold some 5,000 pairs.
- [W26.31] In China, the Mandarin duck has since been designated as a protected species.
- [W26.32] A survey in 2009 estimated the Mandarin duck population in China to be 12,000 – 14,000.
- [W26.33] The Asian populations are migratory, overwintering in lowland eastern China and southern Japan.
- [W26.34] A fossil coracoid from the Middle Pleistocene of West Runton, England, was originally referred to this species and was thought to indicate a formerly much more extensive distribution.
- [W26.35] However this has now been reinterpreted as an indeterminate member of Anatinae.
- [W26.36] Specimens frequently escape from collections, and in the 20th century, a large, feral population was established in Great Britain; more recently, small numbers have bred in Ireland, concentrated in the parks of Dublin.
- [W26.37] Now, about 7,000 are in Britain.
- [W26.38] Owing to its different habitat preferences compared to native water birds, the mandarin duck appears to have had no negative impacts on native wildfowl as a result of its introduction to the UK, as it does not engage in competition with other ducks over their habitats and occupies a previously-vacant ecological niche; it is generally not considered to be invasive.
- [W26.39] However, its expanding range means that it may compete with common goldeneye (Bucephala clangula), which also nests in trees.
- [W26.40] Additional populations of mandarin ducks can be found on the European continent, the largest of which is in the region of Berlin.
- [W26.41] Isolated populations exist in the United States.
- [W26.42] The town of Black Mountain, North Carolina, has a limited population, and a free-flying feral population of several hundred mandarins exist in Sonoma County, California.
- [W26.43] This population is the result of several ducks escaping from captivity, then reproducing in the wild.
- [W26.44] The habitats it prefers in its native breeding range are the dense, shrubby forested edges of rivers and lakes.
- [W26.45] It mostly occurs in low-lying areas, but it may breed in valleys at altitudes of up to 1,500 m (4,900 ft).
- [W26.46] In winter, it additionally occurs in marshes, flooded fields, and open rivers.
- [W26.47] While it prefers fresh water, it may also be seen wintering in coastal lagoons and estuaries.
- [W26.48] In its introduced European range, it lives in more open habitat than in its native range, around the edges of lakes, water meadows, and cultivated areas with woods nearby.
- [W26.49] Compared to other ducks, mandarin ducks are shy birds, preferring to seek cover under trees such as overhanging willows, and form smaller flocks, but when accustomed to humans may exhibit bolder behaviour.
- [W26.50] In the wild, mandarin ducks breed in densely wooded areas near shallow lakes, marshes or ponds.
- [W26.51] They nest in cavities in trees close to water during the spring.
- [W26.52] A single clutch of nine to twelve eggs is laid in April or May.
- [W26.53] Although the male may defend the brooding female and his eggs during incubation, he himself does not incubate the eggs and leaves before they hatch.
- [W26.54] Shortly after the ducklings hatch, their mother flies to the ground and coaxes the ducklings to leap from the nest.
- [W26.55] After all of the ducklings are out of the tree, they will follow their mother to a nearby body of water.
- [W26.56] Mandarins feed by dabbling or walking on land.
- [W26.57] They mainly eat plants and seeds, especially beech mast and acorns.
- [W26.58] The species will also add snails, insects and small fish to its diet.
- [W26.59] The diet of mandarin ducks changes seasonally; in the fall and winter, they mostly eat acorns and grain.
- [W26.60] In the spring, they mostly eat insects, snails, fish and aquatic plants.
- [W26.61] In the summer, they eat small worms, small fish, frogs, mollusks, and small snakes.
- [W26.62] They feed mainly near dawn or dusk, perching in trees or on the ground during the day.
- [W26.63] Conspecific brood parasitism
- [W26.64] Like many other bird species, Mandarin ducks display conspecific brood parasitism.
- [W26.65] Typically, Mandarin ducks lay their eggs in nests of their own relatives or other bird species.
- [W26.66] In the Zuojia Nature Reserve in Northeast China, 46.1% of Mandarin ducks were found to practice conspecific brood parasitism.
- [W26.67] Female ducks lay their eggs in different nests for a wide variety of reasons.
- [W26.68] For example, when there are nest limitations or there are few resources available, female ducks are more likely to practice conspecific brood parasitism.
- [W26.69] When females practice this behavior, they can benefit from a decrease in the costs from parental care and incubation.
- [W26.70] Additionally, female parasitic ducks can reduce their risks from predation.
- [W26.71] While there was speculation that larger clutch sizes can lead to an increase in resource competition, research has found that the number of parasite eggs had no negative influence on the success of eggs from the host.
- [W26.72] Over generations, conspecific brood parasitism can increase the net number of offspring found within each generation.
- [W26.73] Overall, other duck species that have utilised this behaviour to lay their eggs were able to increase their reproductive success by more than double.
- [W26.74] Predation of the mandarin duck varies between different parts of its range.
- [W26.75] Mink, raccoon dogs, otters, polecats, Eurasian eagle-owls, and grass snakes are all predators of the mandarin duck.
- [W26.76] The greatest threat to the mandarin duck is habitat loss due to logging.
- [W26.77] Hunters are also a threat to the mandarin duck, because often they are unable to identify mandarin ducks in flight and as a result, many are shot by accident.
- [W26.78] Mandarin ducks are not hunted for food, but are still poached because their extreme beauty is prized.
- [W26.79] Because of its striking plumage, mandarin ducks are very popular in zoos and waterfowl collections.
- [W26.80] Various mutations and domesticated breeds have been selected in captivity by duck breeders, the most common of which are pale ('silver') and white birds.
- [W26.81] The Chinese refer to mandarin ducks as yuanyang (simplified Chinese: 鸳鸯; traditional Chinese: 鴛鴦; pinyin: yuānyāng), where 'yuan' (鴛) and 'yang' (鴦) respectively stand for male and female mandarin ducks.
- [W26.82] In traditional Chinese culture, mandarin ducks are believed to be lifelong couples, unlike other species of ducks.
- [W26.83] Hence they are regarded as a symbol of conjugal affection and fidelity, and are frequently featured in Chinese art.
- [W26.84] A Chinese proverb for loving couples uses the mandarin duck as a metaphor: "Two mandarin ducks playing in water" (simplified Chinese: 鸳鸯戏水; traditional Chinese: 鴛鴦戲水; pinyin: yuānyāng xì shuǐ).
- [W26.85] A mandarin duck symbol is also used in Chinese weddings because in traditional Chinese lore, they symbolize wedded bliss and fidelity.
- [W26.86] Because the male and female plumages of the mandarin duck are so unalike, 'yuan-yang' is frequently used colloquially in Cantonese to mean an "odd couple" or "unlikely pair" – a mixture of two different types of the same category; for example, the drink yuanyang and yuan-yang fried rice.
- [W26.87] Mandarin ducks featured on the flag of Weihaiwei during British rule.
- [W26.88] For Koreans, mandarin ducks represent peace, fidelity, and plentiful offspring.
- [W26.89] Similar to the Chinese, they believe that these ducks mate for life.
- [W26.90] For these reasons, pairs of wooden-carved mandarin ducks called wedding ducks are often given as wedding gifts and play a significant role in Korean marriage.
- [W26.91] Similarly, in Japanese the ducks are called oshidori (おしどり/オシドリ/鴛鴦) and are used in the phrase oshidori fūfu (おしどり夫婦, "a couple of lovebirds/happily married couple").
- [W26.92] In addition, the Crown Prince wears the Sokutai embroidered with a pattern featuring oshidori.
- [W26.93] Simko-Bednarski, Evan (2 November 2018).
- [W26.94] "A rare Mandarin duck is hanging out in NYC's Central Park and nobody knows how it got there".
