- [W33.55] Some peas lack the tough membrane inside the pod wall and have tender edible pods, allowing them to be eaten whole.
- [W33.56] Snow peas have flat pods with thin pod walls.
- [W33.57] Pods and seeds are eaten when they are very young.
- [W33.58] Snap peas (also known as sugar snap peas) have rounded pods with thick pod walls.
- [W33.59] Pods and seeds are eaten before maturity.
- [W33.60] The name sugar pea can include both types or be synonymous with either snow peas or snap peas in different dictionaries.
- [W33.61] The term mangetout (; from French: pois mange-tout, 'eat-all pea') is generally used in British English to refer to the snow pea specifically, but may also refer to a snap pea, especially when used in other contexts.
- [W33.62] Snow peas and snap peas both belong to macrocarpon group, a cultivar group based on the variety Pisum sativum var. macrocarpum Ser. named in 1825.
- [W33.63] It was described as having very compressed non-leathery edible pods in the original publication.
- [W33.64] The field pea is a type of pea sometimes called Pisum sativum subsp. arvense (L.) Asch.
- [W33.65] It is also known as dun (grey-brown) pea, Kapucijner pea, or Austrian winter pea, and is one of the oldest domesticated crops, cultivated for at least 7,000 years.
- [W33.66] Field peas are now grown in many countries for both human consumption and stockfeed.
- [W33.67] There are several cultivars and colours including blue, dun (brown), maple and white.
- [W33.68] This pea should not be confused with the cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) which is sometimes called the "field pea" in warmer climates.
- [W33.69] It is a climbing annual legume with weak, viny, and relatively succulent stems.
- [W33.70] Vines often are 120–150 cm (4–5 ft) long, but when grown alone, field pea's weak stems prevent it from growing more than 45–60 cm (1+1⁄2–2 ft) tall.
- [W33.71] Leaves have two leaflets and a tendril.
- [W33.72] Flowers are white, pink, or purple.
- [W33.73] Pods carry seeds that are large (seed densities of 8,800/kg or 4,000/lb), nearly spherical, and white, gray, green, or brown.
- [W33.74] The root system is relatively shallow and small, but well nodulated.
- [W33.75] The field pea is a cool-season legume crop that is grown on over 10 million hectares (25 million acres) worldwide.
- [W33.76] It has been an important grain legume crop for millennia, seeds showing domesticated characteristics dating from at least 7,000 years ago have been found in archaeological sites around what is now Turkey.
- [W33.77] Field peas or "dry peas" are marketed as a dry, shelled product for either human or livestock food, unlike the garden pea, which is marketed as a fresh or canned vegetable.
- [W33.78] The major producing countries of field peas are Russia and China, followed by Canada, Europe, Australia and the United States.
- [W33.79] Europe, Australia, Canada and the U.S. raise over 1.8 million hectares (4.4 million acres) and are major exporters of peas.
- [W33.80] In 2002, there were approximately 120,000 hectares (300,000 acres) of field peas grown in the U.S.
- [W33.81] The wild pea is restricted to the Mediterranean Basin and the Near East.
- [W33.82] The earliest archaeological finds of peas date from  about 10'000 B.C.
- [W33.83] Near East and Central Asia.
- [W33.84] In Egypt, early finds date from c.
- [W33.85] 4800–4400 BC in the Nile Delta area, and from c.
- [W33.86] 3800–3600 BC in Upper Egypt.
- [W33.87] In northern Europe, specifically Fennoscandia, findings of pea data back to 4000 BC.
- [W33.88] The pea was also present in Georgia in the 5th millennium BC.
- [W33.89] Farther east, the finds are younger.
- [W33.90] Peas were present in Afghanistan c.
- [W33.91] 2000 BC, in Harappan civilization around modern-day Pakistan and western- and northwestern India in 2250–1750 BC.
- [W33.92] In the second half of the 2nd millennium BC, this legume crop appears in the Ganges Basin and southern India.
- [W33.93] In early times, peas were grown mostly for their dry seeds.
- [W33.94] From plants growing wild in the Mediterranean Basin, constant selection since the Neolithic dawn of agriculture improved their yield.
- [W33.95] Peas are mentioned in Aristophanes's The Birds.
- [W33.96] The Greeks and Romans were cultivating this legume from around 500 BC to 400 BC, with vendors in the streets of Athens selling hot pea soup.
- [W33.97] In the early 3rd century BC, Theophrastus mentions peas among the legumes that are sown late in the winter because of their tenderness.
- [W33.98] In the first and second centuries BC, Cato the Elder and Varro both mention peas in their respective works De agri cultura and De re rustica.
- [W33.99] It is also mentioned frequently in de re coquinaria by Apicius and occurs in many different recipes.
- [W33.100] In the Middle Ages, field peas are constantly mentioned, as they were the staple that kept famine at bay, as Charles the Good, count of Flanders, noted explicitly in 1124.
- [W33.101] Green "garden" peas, eaten immature and fresh, were an innovative luxury of Early Modern Europe.
- [W33.102] In England, the distinction between field peas and garden peas dates from the early 17th century: John Gerard and John Parkinson both mention garden peas.
- [W33.103] Snow and snap peas, which the French called mange-tout, because they were eaten pods and all, were introduced to France from the market gardens of Holland in the time of Henri IV, through the French ambassador.
- [W33.104] Green peas were introduced from Genoa to the court of Louis XIV in January 1660, with some staged fanfare.
- [W33.105] A hamper of them was presented before the King.
- [W33.106] They were shelled by the Savoyan comte de Soissons, who had married a niece of Cardinal Mazarin.
- [W33.107] Little dishes of peas were then presented to the King, the Queen, Cardinal Mazarin and Monsieur, the king's brother.
- [W33.108] Immediately established and grown for earliness warmed with manure and protected under glass, they were still a luxurious delicacy in 1696, when Mme de Maintenon and Mme de Sevigné each reported that they were "a fashion, a fury".
- [W33.109] The first sweet tasting pea was developed in the 18th century by amateur plant breeder Thomas Edward Knight of Downton, near Salisbury, England.
- [W33.110] Modern split peas, with their indigestible skins rubbed off, are a development of the later 19th century.
- [W33.111] The first pea harvesting machine ("pea viner") able to shell peas through impact was invented around 1890 by John Alexander Chisholm.
- [W33.112] Large-scale commercial harvesting of peas without edible pods can be accomplished using specialised pea harvester machines (also called pea viners) that strip them from their vines.
- [W33.113] By contrast, the two edible-pod pea cultivars (snow peas and snap peas) are still usually picked by hand.
- [W33.114] A prototype for an automated snap pea harvester was being researched in 2017.
- [W33.115] Pea grading involves sorting peas by size, in which the smallest peas are graded as the highest quality for their tenderness.
- [W33.116] Brines may be used, in which peas are floated, from which their density can be determined.
- [W33.117] A variety of diseases affect peas through a number of pathogens, including insects, viruses, bacteria and fungi.
- [W33.118] In particular, virus disease of peas has worldwide economic importance.
- [W33.119] Additionally, the diseases limiting to global yield potential of pea are members of the pea root rot complex.
- [W33.120] Additionally, insects such as the pea leaf weevil (Sitona lineatus) can damage peas and other pod fruits.
- [W33.121] The pea leaf weevil is native to Europe, but has spread to other places such as Alberta, Canada.
- [W33.122] They are about 3.5–5.5 mm (9⁄64–7⁄32 in) long and are distinguishable by three light-coloured stripes running length-wise down the thorax.
- [W33.123] The weevil larvae feed on the root nodules of pea plants, which are essential to the plants' supply of nitrogen, and thus diminish leaf and stem growth.
- [W33.124] Adult weevils feed on the leaves and create a notched, "c-shaped" appearance on the outside of the leaves.
- [W33.125] Delia platura, also known as the seed corn maggot, is another pest of peas that can cause damage to germinating seeds and seedlings.
- [W33.126] The pea moth can be a serious pest producing caterpillars that resemble small white maggots in the pea pods.
- [W33.127] The caterpillars eat the developing peas making them unsightly and unsuitable for culinary use.
- [W33.128] Prior to the use of modern insecticides, pea moth caterpillars were a very common sight in pea pods.
- [W33.129] In 2023, world production of green peas was 21.5 million tonnes, led by China and India with 86% of the total when combined (table).
- [W33.130] Some people experience allergic reactions to peas, with vicilin or convicilin as the most common allergens.
- [W33.131] Raw green peas are 79% water, 14% carbohydrates, 5% protein, and contain negligible fat.
- [W33.132] In a reference amount of 100 grams (3+1⁄2 ounces), raw green peas supply 339 kilojoules (81 kilocalories) of food energy, and are a rich source (20% or more of the Daily Value, DV) of vitamin C, vitamin K, and thiamine, with several B vitamins and dietary minerals in moderate amounts (10–18% DV) (table).
- [W33.133] In modern times peas are usually boiled or steamed, which breaks down the cell walls and makes them taste sweeter and the nutrients more bioavailable.
- [W33.134] Along with broad beans and lentils, these formed an important part of the diet of most people in the Middle East, North Africa and Europe during the Middle Ages.
- [W33.135] By the 17th and 18th centuries, it had become popular to eat peas "green", that is, while they are immature and right after they are picked.
- [W33.136] New cultivars of peas were developed by the English during this time, which became known as "garden" or "English" peas.
- [W33.137] The popularity of green peas spread to North America.
- [W33.138] Thomas Jefferson grew more than 30 cultivars of peas on his estate.
- [W33.139] With the invention of canning, peas were one of the first vegetables to be canned.
- [W33.140] Fresh peas are often eaten boiled and flavoured with butter or spearmint as a side dish vegetable.
- [W33.141] Salt and pepper are also commonly added to peas when served.
- [W33.142] Fresh peas are also used in pot pies, salads and casseroles.
- [W33.143] Pod peas (snow peas and snap peas) are used in stir-fried dishes, particularly those in American Chinese cuisine.
- [W33.144] Pea pods do not keep well once picked, and if not used quickly, are best preserved by drying, canning or freezing within a few hours of harvest.
- [W33.145] Dried peas are often made into a soup or simply eaten on their own.
- [W33.146] In Japan, China, Taiwan and some Southeast Asian countries, including Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia, peas are roasted and salted, and eaten as snacks.
- [W33.147] In the Philippines, peas, while still in their pods, are a common ingredient in viands and pansit.
- [W33.148] In the UK, dried yellow or green split peas are used to make pease pudding (or "pease porridge"), a traditional dish.
- [W33.149] In North America, a similarly traditional dish is split pea soup.
- [W33.150] Pea soup is eaten in many other parts of the world, including northern Europe, parts of middle Europe, Russia, Iran, Iraq and India.
- [W33.151] In India, fresh peas are used in various dishes such as aloo matar (curried potatoes with peas) or mattar paneer (paneer cheese with peas), though they can be substituted with frozen peas as well.
- [W33.152] Peas are also eaten raw, as they are sweet when fresh off the bush.
- [W33.153] Green peas known as hasiru batani in Kannada are used to make curry and gasi.
- [W33.154] Split peas are also used to make dal, particularly in Guyana, and Trinidad, where there is a significant population of Indians.
- [W33.155] In Chinese cuisine, the tender new growth (leaves and stem) dou miao (pea shoots, 豆苗; dòu miáo) are commonly used in stir-fries.
- [W33.156] Much like picking the leaves for tea, the farmers pick the tips off of the pea plant.
- [W33.157] In Greece, Tunisia, Turkey, Cyprus, and other parts of the Mediterranean, peas are made into a stew with lamb and potatoes.
- [W33.158] In Hungary and Serbia, pea soup is often served with dumplings and spiced with hot paprika.
- [W33.159] In the United Kingdom, dried, rehydrated and mashed marrowfat peas, or cooked green split peas, known as mushy peas, are popular, originally in the north of England, but now ubiquitously, and especially as an accompaniment to fish and chips or meat pies, particularly in fish and chip shops.
- [W33.160] Sodium bicarbonate is sometimes added to soften the peas.
- [W33.161] In 2005, a poll of 2,000 people revealed the pea to be Britain's seventh favourite culinary vegetable.
- [W33.162] Processed peas are mature peas which have been dried, soaked and then heat treated (processed) to prevent spoilage, in the same manner as pasteurising.
- [W33.163] Cooked peas are sometimes sold dried and coated with wasabi, salt, or other spices.
- [W33.164] In North America pea milk is produced and sold as an alternative to cow milk for a variety of reasons.
- [W33.165] In East Asia, pea sprouts or shoots (豆苗; 완두순) were once dedicated cuisine when the plant was less highly available.
- [W33.166] Today, when the plant can be easily grown, fresh pea shoots are available in supermarkets or may be grown at home.
- [W33.167] In order to freeze and preserve peas, they must first be grown, picked, and shelled.
- [W33.168] Usually, the more tender the peas are, the more likely that they will be used in the final product.
- [W33.169] The peas must be put through the process of freezing shortly after being picked so that they do not spoil too soon.
- [W33.170] Once the peas have been selected, they are placed in ice water and allowed to cool.
- [W33.171] After, they are sprayed with water to remove any residual dirt or dust that may remain on them.
- [W33.172] The next step is blanching.
- [W33.173] The peas are boiled for a few minutes to remove any enzymes that may shorten their shelf life.
- [W33.174] They are then cooled and removed from the water.
- [W33.175] The final step is the actual freezing to produce the final product.
- [W33.176] This step may vary considerably; some companies freeze their peas by air blast freezing, where the vegetables are put through a tunnel at high speeds and frozen by cold air.
- [W33.177] Finally, the peas are packaged and shipped out for retail sale.
- [W33.178] In the mid-19th century, Austrian monk Gregor Mendel's observations of pea pods led to the principles of Mendelian genetics, the foundation of modern genetics.
- [W33.179] He ended up growing and examining about 28,000 pea plants in the course of his experiments.
- [W33.180] Mendel chose peas for his experiments because he could grow them easily, pure-bred strains were readily available, and the structure of the flowers protect them from cross-pollination, and cross pollination was easy.
- [W33.181] Mendel cross-bred tall and dwarf pea plants, green and yellow peas, purple and white flowers, wrinkled and smooth peas, and a few other traits.
- [W33.182] He then observed the resulting offspring.
- [W33.183] In each of these cases, one trait is dominant and all the offspring, or Filial-1 (abbreviated F1) generation, showed the dominant trait.
- [W33.184] Then he allowed the F1 generation to self pollinate and observed their offspring, the Filial-2 (abbreviated F2)  generation.
- [W33.185] The F2 plants had the dominant trait in approximately a 3:1 ratio.
- [W33.186] He studied later generations of self pollinated plants, and performed crosses to determine the nature of the pollen and egg cells.
- [W33.187] Mendel reasoned that each parent had a 'vote' in the appearance of the offspring, and the non-dominant, or recessive, trait appeared only when it was inherited from both parents.
- [W33.188] He did further experiments that showed each trait is separately inherited.
- [W33.189] Unwittingly, Mendel had solved a major problem with Charles Darwin's theory of evolution: how new traits were preserved and not blended back into the population, a question Darwin himself did not answer.
- [W33.190] Mendel's work was published in an obscure Austrian journal and was not rediscovered until about 1900.
- [W33.191] Peas, like many legumes, contain symbiotic bacteria called Rhizobia within root nodules of their root systems.
- [W33.192] These bacteria have the special ability to fix nitrogen from atmospheric, molecular nitrogen (N2) into ammonia (NH3).
- [W33.193] N2 + 8H+ + 8e−  →  2NH3 + H2
- [W33.194] Ammonia is then converted to another form, ammonium (NH+4), usable by (some) plants, by the following reaction:
- [W33.195] The root nodules of peas and other legumes are sources of nitrogen that they can use to make amino acids, constituents of proteins.
- [W33.196] Hence, legumes are good sources of plant protein.
- [W33.197] When a pea plant dies in the field, for example following the harvest, all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into amino acids inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil.
- [W33.198] In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (NO−3), that is available to other plants, thereby serving as fertiliser for future crops.

## [W34] Wikipedia: Experiments on Plant Hybridization
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Experiments_on_Plant_Hybridization&oldid=1376466396 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · usage: ai_input

- [W34.1] "Experiments on Plant Hybridization" (German: Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden) is a seminal paper written in 1865 and published in 1866 by Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar considered to be the founder of modern genetics.
- [W34.2] The paper was the result after years spent studying genetic traits in Pisum sativum, the pea plant.
- [W34.3] In his paper, Mendel compared 7 pairs of discrete traits found in a pea plant:
- [W34.4] Through experimentation, Mendel discovered that one inheritable trait would invariably be dominant to its recessive alternative.
- [W34.5] Mendel laid out the genetic model later known as Mendelian inheritance or Mendelian genetics.
- [W34.6] This model provided an alternative to blending inheritance, which was the prevailing theory at the time.
- [W34.7] Mendel read his paper to the Natural History Society of Brünn.
- [W34.8] It was published in the Proceedings of the Natural History Society of Brünn the following year.
- [W34.9] Mendel's work received little attention from the scientific community and was largely forgotten.
- [W34.10] It was not until the early 20th century that Mendel's work was rediscovered and his ideas used to help form the modern synthesis.
- [W34.11] Mendel had read a 1863 German translation of Darwin's On the Origin of Species (translated by H.G.
- [W34.12] Bronn), and used certain terms from the translation in the final two (10th and 11th) sections of his paper.
- [W34.13] There were three main English translations.
- [W34.14] The first was done in 1901, commissioned by William Bateson to the Royal Horticultural Society of London.
- [W34.15] It was mainly done by Charles Thomas Druery, a British poet, author, and botanist.
- [W34.16] The second was done in 1966 by Curt Stern and Eva Sherwood.
- [W34.17] The third was done in 2016, with a careful adherence to the Darwinian terminologies that had been used by Mendel, and released to the public domain.
- [W34.18] In 1936, the statistician Ronald Fisher used a Pearson's chi-squared test to analyze Mendel's data and concluded that Mendel's results with the predicted ratios were far too perfect, suggesting that adjustments (intentional or unconscious) had been made to the data to make the observations fit the hypothesis.
- [W34.19] Later authors have suggested Fisher's analysis was flawed, proposing various statistical and botanical explanations for Mendel's numbers.
- [W34.20] It is also possible that Mendel's results are "too good" merely because he reported the best subset of his data—Mendel mentioned in his paper that the data were from a subset of his experiments.
- [W34.21] Modern geneticists have inferred the 7 genes studied by Mendel.
- [W34.22] It is impossible to know for certain, but the identification is possible to a high degree of confidence based on Mendel's description, and the pea varieties grown in central Europe in the 1850s.
- [W34.23] The table shows that the 7 genes appeared on 5 chromosomes.
- [W34.24] Of these, the only pair with significant linkage are V and LE, who are 12.6 map units apart.
- [W34.25] The other pair, R and GP, are very weakly linked.
- [W34.26] The effect is that Mendel was unlikely to have encountered genetic linkage.
- [W34.27] In any case, he did not report dihybrid experiments on either of these pairs, and only reported on the unlinked pairs, and he always found the ratio to be 9:3:3:1.
- [W34.28] The 1901 translation:  The full text of Experiments in Plant-Hybridisation at Wikisource
- [W34.29] The 2016 translation: Abbott, Scott; Fairbanks, Daniel J (1 October 2016).
- [W34.30] "Experiments on Plant Hybrids by Gregor Mendel".

## Two-gene rebuild: facts pinned 2026-10-27 (hand-written notes; the drafter's, not an independent check)

The lesson step "Two spots, one egg" and the cases c_2ssd401nns (drake), c_cm3v9gm8ct (flies) and c_nv3fs4gag5 (peas) rest on the sentences below. W25–W34 were fetched on 2026-10-27 with the User-Agent "MapOfKnowledge/1.0 (personal study tool)" and cached in sources/ (W31, Morgan 1916, is the same Gutenberg file genetics-sex-linked already pinned, copied). Short lines (numbers, table cells) under 25 characters are dropped from the numbered sheet by facts.mjs, so the counts below are quoted from the cached files themselves.

### Pairs are dealt separately (the lesson step and every case)
- People: "diploid human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes including 1 pair of sex chromosomes (46 total), half of maternal origin and half of paternal origin" [W1.20]: chromosomes 5 and 11 are two different pairs, one copy of each from each parent.
- "The physical basis of the independent assortment of chromosomes is the random orientation of each bivalent along with the metaphase plate, with respect to the orientation of the other bivalents" [W1.113]; also [W3.79], [W3.130], [W3.131].
- "The law of independent assortment always holds true for genes that are located on different chromosomes" [W4.84]; "genes located on different chromosomes assort independently" [W4.96].
- So at each spot an egg or sperm takes the maternal copy half the time, independently of a spot on another pair: both maternal 1/4, one of each 1/2 (the lesson step); four spots on four pairs all maternal 1/16, all paternal 1/16, together 1/8 (c_2ssd401nns). The engine computes these (cases/engines.ts); none is typed.

### The drake (c_2ssd401nns)
- "A male is called a drake and the female is called a duck" [W25.11].
- "Mandarin duck unusually has 84 chromosomes … compared to 80, often submetacentric, for other ducks" [W26.18]: 80 chromosomes, 40 pairs, in a mallard.
- NCBI's complete (telomere-to-telomere) genome of a Pekin duck, a domestic mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), female: "Chromosomes (nuclear): 1, 2, … 39, W, Z: 39 numbered chromosomes plus the sex chromosomes W and Z" [W27.2], [W27.4]. 39 numbered pairs plus the sex pair is 40 pairs, matching [W26.18]; chromosomes 2, 5, 7 and 9 are four different numbered pairs.
- Not claimed: anything about the Z chromosome; the four spots are on numbered chromosomes.

### The flies (c_cm3v9gm8ct)
- Ebony and vestigial sit on different chromosomes: e (ebony) "Genomic location: chromosome arm 3R" [W29.2] (alias "Ebony" [W29.3]); vg (vestigial) "Genomic location: chromosome arm 2R" [W30.2]. The fly has "three autosomes labeled 2, 3, and 4" [W28.216].
- Ebony needs two copies to show: "e1: Ebony; black body and wings (heterozygotes are also visibly darker than wild type)" [W28.157], listed among markers where "Recessive alleles are in lower case" [W28.155]. So one ebony copy darkens a fly a shade but does not make it ebony; the case counts ebony (black) flies only, which need two copies. Morgan calls the hybrids "gray" (below).
- Vestigial needs two copies to show: "the cross of Drosophila with vestigial wings to the wild type with long wings … The F_1 flies have long wings not differing from those of the wild fly, so far as can be observed. When two such flies are inbred there result three long to one vestigial." [W31.783]–[W31.788]
- The very cross: "A fourth case is shown in the fruit fly, where an ebony fly with long wings is mated to a grey fly with vestigial wings (fig. 24). The offspring are gray with long wings. If these are inbred they give 9 gray long, 3 gray vestigial, 3 ebony long, 1 ebony vestigial" [W31.850]–[W31.853] (Morgan, 1916, under "Mendel's second discovery: independent assortment").
- Vestigial wings: "Vestigial wings are those not fully developed and that have lost function" [W28.194 and the sentence after it].

### The peas (c_nv3fs4gag5)
- Dominance: "Of the differentiating characters which were used in the experiments the following are dominant: The round or roundish form of the seed …" [W32.264]–[W32.265]. The next line of this Wikisource transcription reads "The low colouring of the seed albumen [cotyledons]" [W32.266], a transcription slip for "yellow": the same paper's two-character experiment says "The fertilised seeds appeared round and yellow like those of the seed parents" [W32.514] (the pollen parents were angular and green), and the modern reading lists "Seed shape; Dominant phenotype: Round; Recessive phenotype: Wrinkled" and "Cotyledon color; Dominant phenotype: Yellow; Recessive phenotype: Green" [W34.33], [W34.35]. Morgan 1916 on peas: "Yellow is said therefore to be dominant and green to be recessive" [W31.780].
- Different chromosomes: seed shape R is in linkage group V and cotyledon colour I in linkage group I [W34.33], [W34.35]; "the 7 genes appeared on 5 chromosomes" [W34.23], and Mendel "only reported on the unlinked pairs" [W34.27].
- Self-pollination: "Pea plants can self-pollinate" [W33.24]; in the paper, "the fertilising organs are closely packed inside the keel and the anther bursts within the bud, so that the stigma becomes covered with pollen even before the flower opens" [W32.84]–[W32.88]; also [W18.10].
- Wrinkled: the translation calls the recessive seed form "angular" in the two-character experiment and "angular wrinkled" elsewhere ("The angular wrinkled form of the seed" [W32.299]; "1,850 angular wrinkled" [W32.314]); the case says "wrinkled", as [W34.33] does.
- The real count (cached file, Expt. 1 of the two-character experiments): "In all 556 seeds were yielded by 15 plants, and of these there were :— 315 round and yellow, 101 angular and yellow, 108 round and green, 32 angular and green." [W32.517]–[W32.518] and the lines after. 108 + 101 = 209 mix the grandparents' looks; the engine's expectation is 3/8 × 556 = 208.5. The scenario and reveal never name Mendel; only the source label does.
- Morgan 1916, opening "Mendel's second discovery—independent assortment": "If a pea that is yellow and round is crossed to one that is green and wrinkled (fig. 21), all of the offspring are yellow and round. Inbred, these give 9 yellow round, 3 green round, 3 yellow wrinkled, 1 green wrinkled." [W31.825]–[W31.826] and the cached text after them.
- The paper's conclusion from these crosses: "the relation of each pair of different characters in hybrid union is independent of the other differences in the two original parental stocks" [W32.602].
